Float results are in the type's own format, in the register's low bits.

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text: A vector packs 64 / width elements into one register, with element 0 in the most significant bits. For example, $r1 = 0x0102030405060708, read as ($vi8), holds the eight elements 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, in that order. A vector operation works on every element at once, which is where the engine's speed on small data types comes from: one ($vi8) add is eight additions.

docs.title: Floats
docs.text:
f32 and f64 are IEEE single and double precision. The narrow formats are for low-precision work:

  • f16 is IEEE half precision (5 exponent bits, 10 mantissa bits, bias 15).
  • f8 has 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits (bias 7).
  • f4 holds just the values ±{0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, ∞, NaN}.

Arithmetic on the narrow formats is done in double precision and rounded back to the narrow format with one round bit (round half up on the magnitude), saturating to infinity, and flushing to zero below the smallest subnormal.

docs.title: Bundles
docs.text:
The engine is a VLIW (very long instruction word) machine: instead of discovering parallelism in hardware, it executes bundles of instructions that the program has already grouped to run together. A bundle holds 1, 2, 4, or 8 instructions of 32 bits each, all executed in the same step:

  • Every instruction of a bundle reads the registers as they were before the bundle. So a bundle that copies $r1 into $r2 and $r2 into $r1 swaps them.
  • Memory accesses happen in slot order: a load sees a store of an earlier slot of the same bundle.
  • No two instructions of a bundle may write the same register (the assembler checks this).

docs.title: Sizes and slots
docs.text:
A bundle's size, and which slot each instruction may occupy, follow the hardware's execution lanes:

  • A bundle that holds a branch, call, return, load, store, divide, or square root must have 8 slots. Any other bundle has the smallest power of two (1, 2, 4, or 8) that fits its instructions. Unused slots hold $null.
  • A bundle's address is a multiple of its size.
  • In an 8-slot bundle, a branch, call, or return must be in slot 0, a divide or square root in slot 1 (the engine has one shared divider), and loads and stores in slots 4 to 7 (the memory lanes).

You don't have to arrange any of this by hand. The assembler closes, pads, places, and arranges every bundle (see What the assembler does), and the engine checks the rules when it runs the bundle (exception 7 if one is broken).

In the encoded program, bit 31 of an instruction word is set on the first instruction of each bundle, which is how the engine finds bundle boundaries. Bits [30:26] are the opcode.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: The instructions below are shown in the syntax the assembler accepts. $rd is the destination register, $rs1 and $rs2 the sources, and imm a signed 10-bit immediate (-512 to 511).

docs.title: Arithmetic and logic (scalar)
docs.text:
+  $rd (type) $rs1 $rs2       // also: - * / | & ^ ~| ~& ~^ << >>
+  $rd (type) $rs1 imm

$rd = $rs1 op $rs2 (or $rs1 op imm). ~|, ~&, and ~^ are NOR, NAND, and XNOR.

  • Integer types have every operation. A signed >> is an arithmetic shift, shift counts use their low 6 bits, and / truncates toward zero. Dividing by zero raises exception 1.
  • Float types have only + - * /. Dividing by zero raises exception 2, and a NaN result exception 3.

docs.title: Vector arithmetic
docs.text:
$v + $rd (vtype) $rs1 $rs2                // also: - *
$v + $rd (vtype) $rs1 $rs2 $replicate     // $rs2's low element, used for every element

Element by element: element i of $rd is element i of $rs1 plus element i of $rs2. Integer results wrap around at the element width. With $replicate, every element of $rs1 is combined with the same value, $rs2's lowest element, for example to scale a vector.

docs.title: Dot product and reduction
docs.text:
$dot $rd (vtype) $rs1 $rs2                // the sum of the element products
$dot $accumulate $rd (vtype) $rs1 $rs2    // the same, plus $rd
$vreduce + $rd (vtype) $rs1               // also: * | & ^ ~^

$dot multiplies two vectors element by element and adds up the products. $vreduce combines all the elements of one vector with one operation. Integer dot products and reductions give a 64-bit result. Float ones give an f32, accumulated in single precision, one element at a time.

docs.title: Square root
docs.text:
$fsqrt $rd ($f32) $rs1                    // or ($f64)

A negative operand raises exception 5.

docs.title: Casts
docs.text:
$cast (dtype) $rd (stype) $rs2

Converts $rs2, of type stype, to type dtype. Both types are scalars, or both are vectors.

  • A scalar cast converts the low bits of $rs2. Between integers, the value is sign- or zero-extended by the source type, then truncated to the destination width. Between integers and floats, the value is converted. A float-to-integer conversion truncates toward zero and saturates, and a NaN gives 0.
  • A vector cast converts every element, and may change the element width by one step at most ($vi8 to $vi16, for example, but not to $vi32). Widening doubles the data, so it writes two registers, $rd and $rd+1. Narrowing reads two, $rs2 and $rs2+1.

docs.title: Moving and arranging bits
docs.text:
$set   $rd index value          // $rd = value << (8*index); value 16 bits, index 0 to 7
$slice $rd high low $rs2        // $rd = bits [high:low] of $rs2
$pack  P $rd W $rs2             // the low W bits of $rs2, $rs2+1, ... packed into P bits
$cmov  (type) $rs1 cond [incr] $rd $rs2   // if $rs2 cond 0, then $rd = $rs1
  • $set loads a constant. value may be decimal, or hexadecimal written _h1234.
  • $pack gathers fields from consecutive registers: $pack 64 $r8 16 $r2 builds $r8 from the low 16 bits of $r2, $r3, $r4, and $r5, with $r2's field in the most significant position. A P larger than 64 writes P/64 registers.
  • $cmov is a conditional move. It tests its last register, $rs2, against 0. An optional increment (++1, --1, --2) is added to $rs2 after the test, which makes $cmov useful as a loop step too.

The conditions, for $cmov and for branches, compare a value with 0: == > < >= <= !=. Signed integers compare as values of the type's width, unsigned integers as 64-bit unsigned values, and floats by value (a NaN satisfies only !=).

docs.title: Loads and stores
docs.text:
$ld (type) $rd [$rs1 + $rs2]        $st (type) [$rs1 + $rs2] $rd
$ld (type) $rd [$rs1 + $rs2 ++n]    // then $rs2 += n * the transfer size (n: -16 to 15)
$ld (type) $rd [$rs1 + imm]

The address is $rs1 + $rs2 (or $rs1 + imm), and must be a multiple of the transfer size (exception 6 otherwise). The ++n form also steps $rs2 on, for walking through an array.

  • 1-, 2-, 4-, and 8-byte transfers move one register. Signed loads sign-extend.
  • $u128 and $u256 move 2 and 4 registers, from $rd upward.
  • A vector type moves one element.

docs.title: Control transfer
docs.text:
? (type) $rs2 cond [incr] $goto label   // branch if $rs2 cond 0; then $rs2 += incr
$call label                             // or $call $rs2: the target is this address + $rs2
$return
$halt
$null

Branch and call targets are relative to the instruction's own address. $call pushes the address of the next bundle onto the RAS, and $return pops it. A branch's optional increment is -2 to 1, and is not allowed with a float test type. Like $cmov's, it lets one instruction both count a loop down and test it.

$halt stops the thread. $null does nothing, and fills the unused slots of a bundle.

docs.title: Encodings
docs.text:
The field layouts, as the assembler writes them. In every instruction word, bit 31 is the bundle start bit and bits [30:26] the opcode.

Instruction Opcode Fields ALU 0x04-0x0F type[25:21] rd[20:16] rs1[15:11] imm-flag[10] rs2[4:0] or imm10[9:0] VALU (ALU) as ALU, with a vector type, and replicate[10] FSQRT 0x10 type rd rs1 DOT 0x11 type rd rs1 accumulate[10] rs2 CAST 0x12 dest type[25:21] rd source type[14:10] rs2 LOAD, STORE 0x13, 0x14 type rd rs1 imm-flag[10] incr[9:5] rs2, or imm10[9:0] SET 0x15 byte index[23:21] rd value[15:0] VREDUCE 0x16 type rd rs1 operation[10:6] (an ALU opcode) CMOV 0x17 type rd rs1 cond[10:8] incr[7:6] rs2 PACK 0x18 rd log2(P)[15:12] log2(W)[11:9] rs2 SLICE 0x19 high[5:1] in [25:21], rd, high[0] in [15], low[14:9], rs2 BRANCH 0x02 type[25:22] cond[21:19] incr[18:17] offset12[16:5] rs2 CALL 0x01 label-flag[25], offset25[24:0] or rs2 RETURN, NULL, HALT 0x03, 0x1A, 0x1B

ALU opcodes: + 0x04, - 0x05, * 0x06, / 0x07, | 0x08, & 0x09, ^ 0x0A, ~| 0x0B, ~& 0x0C, ~^ 0x0D, << 0x0E, >> 0x0F.

Type codes: $i4..$i64 0x00-0x04, $u4..$u64 0x05-0x09, $f4..$f64 0x0A-0x0E, $u128 0x0F, $u256 0x10, $vu4..$vu32 0x11-0x14, $vf4..$vf32 0x15-0x18, $vi4..$vi32 0x19-0x1C.

docs.title: Writing and Running APARA Programs
docs.text:
The apara configuration is one APARA engine on its own, with no SPARC core around it. It is the place to write, run, and debug engine programs, and to study the engine's timing, before using the engine from a SPARC program (see The Engine in a System).

A run works like this: the simulator places the program in the engine's IMEM, the initial data in its DMEM, and the initial register values in its registers, starts one or more threads, and runs until every thread it started has stopped. It then reports how each thread stopped, and, if given the expected final state, checks it.

Like every configuration, apara comes as a fast functional model (cpp_model) and a cycle-level timing model (sitar_model), with the same command line.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
From the repo root:

model/system_models/apara/cpp_model/build.sh      # executable/apara_sim_cpp
model/system_models/apara/sitar_model/build.sh    # executable/apara_sim_sitar (needs the sitar CLI)

docs.title: Running a program
docs.text:
Assemble the program (see APARA Assembly Language and Tools), then run the object file:

python3 compiler/apara/apara_as.py prog.mcode
model/system_models/apara/cpp_model/executable/apara_sim_cpp \
        -p 0x0 -i prog.obj -d data.map -a registers.txt -r results.txt

The options:

Option Meaning -p <pc> Start a thread at <pc> (hexadecimal, an IMEM word index). Repeat it to start threads 1, 2, and 3 too. Without -p, one thread starts at 0. -i <file> The object file. -d <file> DMEM's initial contents (a data file). -a <file> Initial register values. -r <file> The expected final state. The run prints PASS, or the mismatches and FAIL. --dump-results <file> Write the final state as a results file (- for the screen). --stats Print statistics: per-thread counts (cpp_model), or the pipeline's counters (sitar_model, see APARA Timing Model). --trace Print every bundle executed (cpp_model). --max-bundles <n> / --max-cycles <n> Stop a run that does not end on its own (cpp_model / sitar_model). --latency-file <file> Change instruction latencies (sitar_model, see APARA Timing Model).

The file formats are described in File formats.

The exit status is 0 for PASS, or, without -r, when every thread stopped with $halt. It is 1 otherwise (a mismatch, an exception, or a thread still running at the limit), and 2 for an error in the command line or the files. That makes the simulators easy to use from scripts.

docs.title: Watching a program run
docs.text:
--trace prints one line per bundle executed: its thread and address, its instructions (without the $nulls), and, if it did not continue to the next bundle, where it went. For example, the end of a loop, from validation/apara/isa/control/control.mcode:

t0 0x0:  ? ($i64) $r1 > --1 $goto pc+0;  + $r2 ($i64) $r2 $r1;  -> 0x0
t0 0x0:  ? ($i64) $r1 > --1 $goto pc+0;  + $r2 ($i64) $r2 $r1;
t0 0x8:  ? ($f32) $r3 < $goto pc+16;  -> 0x18
t0 0x18:  ? ($i16) $r4 < $goto pc+16;  + $r5 ($i64) $r0 1;  -> 0x28
t0 0x28:  $call pc+32;  + $r10 ($i64) $r0 16;  -> 0x48

The bundle at 0x0 branches back to itself while $r1 is above 0, counting $r1 down each time. On its last pass the branch is not taken, and the thread falls through to 0x8.

A thread that stops on an exception is reported with the slot and the cause:

thread 1: stopped at 0x8 by an exception: slot 4 unaligned memory address;

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
The engine's own test suites are in validation/apara/, with their own runner. APARA Validation Suite describes what the suites contain, the format of a test, how to run the suites on both models, and how to add a test. The following command runs every suite on the C++ model:

cd $SPARC_HOME
python3 validation/apara/run_tests.py

docs.title: Hazards
docs.text:
A hazard is a bundle reading a register before an older bundle of the same thread has written its new value. The engine's pipeline resolves every such read-after-write dependence in hardware: DECODE tells REGFILE which registers a bundle reads and writes, and REGFILE holds a bundle until every register it reads or writes has been written back by the older bundles (see Register locks and tokens). A program, or a compiler, never needs to insert waits.

The other orderings are safe too:

  • Write after write: the same locks hold a bundle that writes a register an older bundle has yet to write, so the newer value always lands last.
  • Write after read: a bundle reads its registers when it is issued, in order, so a later bundle's write can never reach it.
  • Memory: a thread's loads and stores reach DMEM in program order.
  • Other threads: each thread has its own registers.

What the hardware does not resolve is within a single bundle: two instructions writing the same register (directly, or through a multi-register load, a cast's second register, or an increment). Every instruction of a bundle reads the registers as they were before the bundle, so a value written in a bundle cannot be read in the same bundle. The assembler rejects a register written twice (the asm_errors/ tests).

The timing model checks the interlock on every run, in two ways, and --stats reports both:

  • The lock masks. The registers each bundle actually reads and writes when it executes must be among those DECODE locked for it. Otherwise the model prints an internal error, since the interlock would have missed a dependence, and counts a lock-mask violation (lock-mask violations 0 otherwise). The test runner fails a test with any.
  • A hazard count, kept apart from the locks: a bundle issued while a register it reads still has an older write outstanding. With the interlock it must be 0 (RAW hazards 0).

The hazards/ tests check that the interlock is needed where it acts. Built with the knob engine.regfile.interlock = false (in model/system_models/apara/sitar_model/src/Top.sitar, see Knobs), REGFILE ignores its locks, and each hazards/ test must report exactly its HAZARDS_UNLOCKED count: the reads that would get a stale value without the interlock. The tests of independent bundles, write-after-write, and memory order must report none. Run them that way with --sitar: the runner then checks only the hazard counts, since the timing is no longer the engine's. Set the knob back to true, and rebuild, afterwards.

docs.title: The APARA Engine in a System (sparc_apara)
docs.text:
The sparc_apara configuration is a complete system with one SPARC processor and one APARA engine. It is also called the 1p1e system. The SPARC core is the one of core_l1cache_mmu_devices, with its L1 caches, MMU and peripheral devices, and the engine sits beside it as an accelerator. The SPARC program does the general-purpose work, and hands regular, vector-heavy work to the engine.

This page describes the hardware of the system. It lists the components, shows how they are connected, and describes the address map, the engine's control unit and DMA unit, and its interrupt. It ends with how the two models implement the system. The software side, which covers how a SPARC program uses the engine and how to write such a program, is described in Programming the System.

docs.title: The components
docs.text:
The system has the following components:

  • The SPARC V8 core, with its instruction and data L1 caches and its MMU. It runs the main program, a bare-metal C program.
  • Main memory, 256 MB, which holds the SPARC program and its data.
  • The peripheral devices, which are a timer, a serial device, and the Interrupt Controller. The engine's interrupt reaches the SPARC through the Interrupt Controller.
  • The system bus, which joins all of the above. It has two masters, the SPARC core and the engine, and carries one transaction at a time.
  • The APARA engine, with its five-stage pipeline, its four hardware threads, its 16 KB instruction memory (IMEM) and its 64 KB data memory (DMEM). See The engine at a glance for a block diagram of the engine itself.
  • The engine's control unit (CCU). Its memory-mapped registers let the SPARC load IMEM, set a thread's registers, and start, reset or query a thread.
  • The engine's DMA unit. It has four channels, which copy data between main memory and DMEM while the SPARC and the engine both go on working.

The control unit and the DMA unit form the engine's host side, the part that faces the system. The engine's pipeline and memories are the same as in the standalone apara configuration.

docs.title: How the parts are connected
docs.text:
The SPARC core reaches main memory, the devices and the engine through the system bus. The engine is the bus's second master. Its DMA unit, and its own loads and stores outside DMEM, reach main memory through the bus too.

The SPARC and the engine communicate in four ways:

  • Commands, from the SPARC. Writes to the control unit's registers load IMEM, set a thread's registers, and start, reset or query a thread (see The control unit). Writes to the DMA unit's registers start copies (see The DMA unit).
  • Data in DMEM, which the SPARC reads and writes directly through its window in the system's address space, or has the DMA unit copy.
  • Data in main memory, which the engine's own loads and stores, and its DMA unit, reach over the bus as its second master.
  • Completion, from the engine. A thread that stops, with $halt or an exception, leaves a completion word for the SPARC to poll. The control unit can also raise an interrupt, which reaches the SPARC as IRL 14 through the Interrupt Controller. A DMA channel that finishes can do the same.

The engine's threads share its IMEM, DMEM and pipeline. Each thread has its own 32 registers, PC, return-address stack, and ERROR register.

In the timing model, these parts are modules joined by nets (see The models):

docs.title: Address map
docs.text:
The system's physical addresses are as follows:

Range What 0x0000_0000 .. Main memory (256 MB), except for the DMEM window below. 0x0100_0000 .. 0x0100_FFFF The engine's DMEM, 64 KB. 0xFFFE_0000 .. 0xFFFE_007F The engine's control unit (CCU) registers. 0xFFFE_2000 .. 0xFFFE_207F The engine's DMA registers. 0xFFFF_0000 .. 0xFFFF_FFFF The peripheral devices.

These three ranges, DMEM, the CCU registers and the DMA registers, are the engine's three windows. Only main memory is ever cached, and the engine's windows never are. A SPARC program should reach the windows with MMU-bypass accesses (ASI 0x20), as the routines in Programming the System do. The DMEM window lies inside main memory's range, so a program's own code and data must stay clear of it.

docs.title: The engine's own view
docs.text:
Inside the engine, an address in its own DMEM window is local, and every other address goes off island, out to the system, as in the hardware. In a system, an engine program therefore addresses its DMEM by the window's address. Usually the SPARC program passes that address in a register, for example in $r9:

// $r9 = 0x01000000 (set by the SPARC). DMEM byte 0x100 is $r9 + 256.
    || $st ($i64) [$r9 + 256] $r3 ;

An engine load or store to any other address reaches main memory, or a device, through the system bus. Such an access takes much longer than a DMEM access. The standalone apara configuration instead maps every address into DMEM.

docs.title: The control unit
docs.text:
The control unit has a block of 8 32-bit registers for each of the engine's four threads, at 0xFFFE_0000 + 32*thread + 4*register. Commands for a thread go through its block.

Register Contents R0 Control. Bits [31:16] are a sequence number, [15:14] a thread number (for command 9), and [11:8] the command. The flags are [4] run the command interpreter, [3] interrupt enable, [2] completed, [1] started, and [0] start. Bits [7:5], "init done" and "cpu mode" in the hardware, are kept but have no effect in the model. R1 PC R2 IMEM index, or register number R3 IMEM write data, or timer high R4 IMEM read data, or timer low R5 Completion. Bit [31] is valid, [26] RAS error, [25] halt, [24] exception, and [23:0] the exception codes. R6 Register high, or stop PC, or RAS depth R7 Register low, or next PC, or RAS top

To give a command, the host writes its arguments into R1 to R7. It then writes R0 with the command and the flags start and run the command interpreter. The unit sets started, carries the command out, writes its results into the registers, and sets completed. The host polls R0 for completed before it reads the results or gives the next command.

Command Does 1 read IMEM R4 := IMEM[R2] 2 write IMEM IMEM[R2] := R3. IMEM is shared by the threads, so any thread's block will do. 3 reset Stops the thread. Its PC becomes 0, its RAS and ERROR are cleared, and its registers are kept. 4 run Starts the thread at R1. 5 read register R6:R7 := register R2 (high:low) 6 write register register R2 := R6:R7 7 completion Once the thread has stopped, R5 := valid plus its ERROR, and R6 := its PC. Each stop is reported once. Before the stop, R5 := 0. With interrupt enable set, the command instead waits for the stop, and then raises the engine interrupt. 8 step Runs one bundle at R1, with local data only. R7 := the next PC. 9 RAS state R6 := depth, and R7 := top, of the RAS of the thread named in R0[15:14]. 10 timer R3:R4 := the engine's cycle count.

Writing R0 with interrupt enable clear clears the interrupt.

docs.title: The DMA unit
docs.text:
The DMA unit copies data between main memory and DMEM, while the SPARC and the engine both go on working. It has four independent channels, each with 8 registers at 0xFFFE_2000 + 32*channel + 4*register:

Register Contents R0 Control. Bits [31:24] are the operation (1 load, from main memory to DMEM, or 2 store, from DMEM to main memory). Bits [23:20] and [19:16] are the top 4 bits of the 36-bit source and destination addresses, and [15:8] a sequence number. The flags are [4] error, [3] interrupt enable, [2] completed, [1] started, and [0] scheduled. R1, R2 Source and destination base addresses. R3 Total bytes (for the record only). R4 Number of bursts. R5 Gap, the distance between bursts. R6 Bytes per burst. Once completed, the stop cycle. R7 The start cycle.

The host writes R1 to R6, then writes R0 with the operation and scheduled, which starts the channel. A copy is a number of bursts, so one command can also collect or spread out strided data:

  • A load gathers. Burst i comes from source + i·gap, and lands at destination + i·(bytes per burst), so the bursts end up packed together in DMEM.
  • A store scatters, the reverse. The data is packed in DMEM, and spread out in main memory.

One contiguous copy is a single burst. The DMEM-side address may be a DMEM byte offset or a window address. When the copy is done, the channel sets completed, and raises the engine interrupt if interrupt enable was set. Writing R0 with interrupt enable clear clears the interrupt. An unknown operation completes at once, with error set.

docs.title: Interrupts
docs.text:
Both units can interrupt the SPARC when something finishes. The control unit does so when a thread stops (command 7 with interrupt enable), and the DMA unit when a channel completes. Either one drives the Interrupt Controller's external input, IRL 14 (EXTERNAL_IRL). The Interrupt Controller then passes the interrupt to the SPARC core, as for any other device.

How a SPARC program takes this interrupt is described in Programming the System.

docs.title: The models
docs.text:
Both models carry out the same commands with the same C++ classes, AparaControlCore (the control unit), AparaDmaCore (the DMA unit), and AparaCore, the engine itself. As in every configuration, they differ in timing.

  • cpp_model The bus routes the engine's three windows to the engine, and the engine's off-island accesses and DMA transfers go back through the same bus. After every SPARC instruction, the engine runs one bundle, and the DMA unit moves one piece of a copy (up to 8 bytes).
  • sitar_model The engine's pipeline (AparaEngine, see APARA Timing Model) and its host side (AparaHost, the control and DMA units) are modules beside the core. The bus becomes an interconnect with two masters, the core and the host side, taken round robin. See Modules and nets below.

In the sitar_model, the parts divide the work as follows:

Module Owns, does engine.exec The engine's state. Serves the host side's requests (DMEM, registers, IMEM, thread commands), one per cycle. Sends a bundle's off-island loads and stores to the host side, and holds the bundle until they are answered. Tells the host side when a thread stops. host The control unit's and DMA unit's registers and commands. Answers the SPARC's accesses to the engine's three windows, and sends DMA transfers and off-island accesses onto the bus. interconnect One transaction at a time, from the core or from the host side, to main memory, the devices, or the host side.

Every net crossing takes a cycle. A SPARC access to a control-unit register therefore crosses four nets, from the core to the interconnect to the host side and back. An access to DMEM crosses six, since it also goes on to engine.exec, which owns DMEM.

docs.title: Modules and nets
docs.text:
System is that of core_l1cache_mmu_devices, with engine and host added, and its bridge replaced by the two-master interconnect. The engine module is the same AparaEngine as in the apara configuration (see APARA Timing Model). The interconnect routes the SPARC's accesses to the engine's three windows to host, and carries host's DMA transfers and off-island accesses as its second master.

host reaches the engine's state in exec over five more nets. One pair carries its requests to the engine (read a register, write IMEM, start a thread, and so on). A second pair carries the engine's loads and stores that leave it. The fifth net carries the notice that a thread has stopped. The engine's interrupt goes from host to the Interrupt Controller's external input, IRL 14.

Top
 |
 +-- System (module)
      |
      +-- core : Core (module)
      |    |
      |    +-- sparcThread : SparcThread (procedure)
      |    |
      |    +-- caches : L1Caches (procedure)
      |    |
      |    +-- mmu : Mmu (procedure)
      |
      +-- interconnect : SystemInterconnect<2> (module)
      |
      +-- mainMemory : PhysicalMainMemory (module)
      |
      +-- devices : PeripheralDevices (module)
      |
      +-- engine : AparaEngine (module: fetch, decode, regfile, exec, writeback, as in apara)
      |
      +-- host : AparaHost (module)

The table below lists the nets of System. Each net carries data from an output port to an input port.

Net From To coreRequestNet core.requestOut interconnect.masterRequestIn[0] coreResponseNet interconnect.masterResponseOut[0] core.responseIn hostRequestNet host.masterRequestOut interconnect.masterRequestIn[1] hostResponseNet interconnect.masterResponseOut[1] host.masterResponseIn memoryRequestNet interconnect.memoryRequestOut mainMemory.requestIn memoryResponseNet mainMemory.responseOut interconnect.memoryResponseIn devicesRequestNet interconnect.devicesRequestOut devices.requestIn devicesResponseNet devices.responseOut interconnect.devicesResponseIn engineRequestNet interconnect.engineRequestOut host.slaveRequestIn engineResponseNet host.slaveResponseOut interconnect.engineResponseIn interruptLevelNet devices.interruptLevelOut[0] core.interruptLevelIn engineInterruptNet host.interruptOut devices.externalInterruptIn serviceRequestNet host.serviceOut engine.exec.serviceIn serviceResponseNet engine.exec.serviceOut host.serviceIn offIslandRequestNet engine.exec.offIslandOut host.offIslandIn offIslandResponseNet host.offIslandOut engine.exec.offIslandIn stopNet engine.exec.stopOut host.stopIn

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Programming the System describes how a SPARC program uses the engine. It walks through an existing program, lists the ready-made routines, and builds a new program step by step.

docs.title: Programming the System (sparc_apara)
docs.text:
This page describes the software side of the sparc_apara system, which consists of one SPARC core and one APARA engine. It first explains what a program for the system consists of. It then walks through an existing program that offloads a dot product to the engine, and lists the ready-made routines that a SPARC program uses to drive the engine. After the rules for setting up and running the engine, it builds a new program step by step, which can serve as the starting point for further programs. The hardware that these programs use is described in The Engine in a System.

The commands on this page use $SPARC_HOME, the repository's folder, as set in step 2 of Installation.

docs.title: The parts of a program
docs.text:
A program for the system has two parts:

  • A SPARC program, a bare-metal C program like those in Writing and Running C Programs. It is the main program. It prepares the data, hands the work to the engine, and collects the results.
  • One or more engine programs, written in mcode (see APARA Assembly Language and Tools) or in C (see The C Compiler). Each one is the work that the engine does.

The system has no disk, so the engine program travels inside the SPARC program, as a C array. The tool compiler/apara/apara_obj_to_c.py assembles an engine program and writes it as a C header. The SPARC program includes this header, and at run time copies the array into the engine's IMEM. A program is therefore built in two steps:

  1. apara_obj_to_c.py kernel.mcode writes kernel.mcode.h, the engine program as a C array.
  2. compile_c.sh main.c compiles the SPARC program, which includes kernel.mcode.h, into a memory image, main.hex.

The memory image is then run on either model of the sparc_apara configuration, in the same way as any other SPARC program.

docs.title: An example: offloading a dot product
docs.text: The test validation/sparc_apara/basic/dma_dot_product/ offloads a dot product of two 32-element int8_t vectors to the engine. Its memory image is already built, so it runs without a cross-toolchain.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The following commands build the C++ model of sparc_apara, and run the test's memory image on it:

cd $SPARC_HOME/model/system_models/sparc_apara/cpp_model
./build.sh
./executable/sparc_sim_cpp_sparc_apara $SPARC_HOME/validation/sparc_apara/basic/dma_dot_product/dma_dot_product.hex

The run ends with the processor's final state. The lines that matter are the following:

PROCESSOR STATE: ERROR
...
o0 0x1
o1 0xf
...
Simulation halted after 9793 cycles.

The test reports in the same way as the device tests. %o0 is 1 if every check passed, and %o1 has one bit per check. Here all four checks passed, so %o1 is 0xf. The state ERROR is how every program in this repository halts.

The Sitar model is built and run in the same way, in its own folder. With --stats, it also prints the engine's pipeline counters:

cd $SPARC_HOME/model/system_models/sparc_apara/sitar_model
./build.sh
./executable/sparc_sim_sitar_sparc_apara $SPARC_HOME/validation/sparc_apara/basic/dma_dot_product/dma_dot_product.hex --stats

...
APARA engine:
bundles fetched          15
bundles executed         8
bundles skipped          7  (wrong path or stopped thread)
...
register-lock stalls     11 cycles
REGFILE token stalls     2 cycles
DMEM bank conflicts      6
...
Simulation halted after 62470 cycles.

The Sitar model counts clock cycles of the modeled hardware, including every bus transaction of the SPARC's commands and of the DMA copies. The C++ model counts SPARC instructions, so its count is much smaller.

docs.title: The engine program
docs.text:
The engine program, kernel.mcode, loads both vectors from DMEM, computes four 8-element dot products in one bundle, adds them up, and stores the 64-bit result back in DMEM:

// The dot product of two 32-element $i8 vectors in DMEM (at $r9 and
// $r10), stored as a 64-bit word at $r9 + 504. ($r9: DMEM's window
// address.)
start:
    ||
        $ld ($i64) $r1 [$r9 + 0]   $ld ($i64) $r2 [$r9 + 8]
        $ld ($i64) $r3 [$r9 + 16]  $ld ($i64) $r4 [$r9 + 24]
    ;
    ||
        $ld ($i64) $r5 [$r10 + 0]   $ld ($i64) $r6 [$r10 + 8]
        $ld ($i64) $r7 [$r10 + 16]  $ld ($i64) $r8 [$r10 + 24]
    ;
    ||
        $dot $r20 ($vi8) $r1 $r5   $dot $r21 ($vi8) $r2 $r6
        $dot $r22 ($vi8) $r3 $r7   $dot $r23 ($vi8) $r4 $r8
    ;
    || + $r24 ($i64) $r20 $r21   + $r25 ($i64) $r22 $r23 ;
    || + $r26 ($i64) $r24 $r25 ;
    || $st ($i64) [$r9 + 504] $r26 ;
    || $halt ;

Each line that starts with || is one bundle, whose instructions run together.

  1. The first two bundles each load four 64-bit words, which is 32 bytes. The first loads vector a from $r9 into $r1 to $r4, and the second loads vector b from $r10 into $r5 to $r8.
  2. The third bundle computes four dot products at once. Each $dot treats its two registers as eight $i8 elements (the type ($vi8)), and adds up their eight products.
  3. The next two bundles add the four partial sums into one.
  4. The sixth bundle stores the result at $r9 + 504, and the last one stops the thread with $halt.

The program never names a fixed address. The SPARC program passes the addresses of the two vectors in $r9 and $r10. These addresses are in DMEM's window, so the engine's loads and stores stay local (see The engine's own view).

docs.title: The SPARC program
docs.text:
The SPARC program, dma_dot_product.c, is the following:

// dma_dot_product.c
//
// A whole offload: two vectors from main memory into the engine's DMEM by
// DMA (two channels at once), the engine's dot product, the result back
// to main memory by DMA.
//   0. both DMA loads complete without error
//   1. the engine stops normally
//   2. the DMA store completes without error
//   3. the result in main memory is the SPARC's own dot product

#include "../../apara_common.h"
#include "kernel.mcode.h"

#define N 32
int8_t a[N] __attribute__((aligned(8)));
int8_t b[N] __attribute__((aligned(8)));
volatile uint32_t result[2] __attribute__((aligned(8)));

int main(void)
{
    uint32_t ok = 0;
    int i, expected = 0;
    for (i = 0; i < N; i++)
    {
        a[i] = (int8_t) (i - 10);
        b[i] = (int8_t) (3 * i - 50);
        expected += a[i] * b[i];
    }

    apara_load_program(kernel_program, KERNEL_PROGRAM_WORDS);
    apara_dma_start(0, APARA_DMA_LOAD, (uint32_t) a, 0, 1, 0, N, 0);
    apara_dma_start(1, APARA_DMA_LOAD, (uint32_t) b, 256, 1, 0, N, 0);
    uint32_t s0 = apara_dma_wait(0), s1 = apara_dma_wait(1);
    if (!(s0 & APARA_DMA_FLAG_ERROR) && !(s1 & APARA_DMA_FLAG_ERROR)) ok |= 1 << 0;

    apara_write_thread_register(0, 9, APARA_DMEM_BASE);
    apara_write_thread_register(0, 10, APARA_DMEM_BASE + 256);
    apara_start_thread(0, KERNEL_START);
    if (apara_wait_thread(0) == (APARA_COMPLETION_VALID | APARA_ERROR_HALT)) ok |= 1 << 1;

    if (!(apara_dma_store(2, (uint32_t) result, 504, 8) & APARA_DMA_FLAG_ERROR)) ok |= 1 << 2;
    uint32_t hi = physical_word(&result[0]), lo = physical_word(&result[1]);
    if (lo == (uint32_t) expected && hi == (expected < 0 ? 0xffffffffu : 0)) ok |= 1 << 3;

    report_and_halt(ok, 4);
    return 0;
}

It follows the five steps that every offload takes:

  1. Load the engine program. apara_load_program copies kernel_program[], from the generated header kernel.mcode.h, into IMEM.
  2. Move the input data into DMEM. Two DMA channels copy the two vectors from main memory at the same time. Channel 0 copies a to DMEM offset 0, and channel 1 copies b to offset 256. apara_dma_wait waits for each channel, and returns its status.
  3. Set the thread's registers, and start it. $r9 and $r10 get the window addresses of the two vectors. apara_start_thread starts thread 0 at KERNEL_START, the address of the label start, which the header defines.
  4. Wait for the thread to stop. apara_wait_thread polls the control unit until the thread stops, and returns its completion word. A thread that ended with $halt reports APARA_COMPLETION_VALID | APARA_ERROR_HALT.
  5. Move the results back. A third DMA channel copies the 8-byte result from DMEM offset 504 to result[] in main memory.

The SPARC program computes the expected dot product itself, and compares it with the engine's. The SPARC has no 64-bit multiply, so it checks the result as two 32-bit halves. It reads them with physical_word, an MMU-bypass load, because the DMA unit's write to main memory does not reach the SPARC's data cache (see The SPARC's data cache). Two helpers come from the suite's shared header, validation/sparc_apara/apara_common.h. These are physical_word, and report_and_halt, which writes the result to %o0 and %o1 and halts.

docs.title: The routines
docs.text:
compiler/include/apara_access_routines.h provides C routines for every step of an offload, in the same style as the device routines of ajit_access_routines.h (see Writing and Running C Programs). The header is on the compiler's include path, so a SPARC program includes it by name:

#include "apara_access_routines.h"

Every routine uses MMU-bypass accesses. A routine therefore works whether or not the MMU is enabled, and never goes through the caches.

Routine Does apara_load_program(words, n) Writes words 0 to n-1 of IMEM. apara_write_imem(i, w), apara_read_imem(i) Write or read one IMEM word. apara_write_thread_register(t, r, v), apara_read_thread_register(t, r) Write or read a thread's 64-bit register. apara_start_thread(t, pc) Starts thread t at pc, a label's address from the program's header. apara_reset_thread(t) Stops thread t, and clears its PC, return-address stack, and ERROR. Its registers are kept. apara_poll_thread(t) Returns the thread's completion word. This is 0 while it is running, or valid plus its ERROR once it has stopped. Each stop is reported once. apara_wait_thread(t) Polls until the thread stops, and returns its completion word. apara_thread_stop_pc(t) Returns where the thread stopped. apara_request_completion_interrupt(t), apara_thread_completion(t), apara_clear_interrupt(t) Learn of a stop by interrupt instead (see Polling or an interrupt). apara_dma_start(c, op, src, dst, bursts, gap, bytes_per_burst, irq) Starts DMA channel c (see The DMA unit). apara_dma_done(c), apara_dma_wait(c) Whether channel c has finished, and waiting for it. apara_dma_load(c, dmem, src, n), apara_dma_store(c, dst, dmem, n) One contiguous copy of n bytes into or out of DMEM, waiting for it to finish. apara_dma_clear_interrupt(c) Clears channel c's interrupt. apara_dmem_write_word(o, v), apara_dmem_read_word(o) Write or read a 32-bit word of DMEM at byte offset o, directly. apara_dmem_read_dword(o) Reads a 64-bit word of DMEM. The high half is at the lower address. apara_load_dmem_image(pairs, n) Writes a C engine program's initialized globals into DMEM (see Carrying the engine's program). apara_read_timer() Returns the engine's cycle counter.

The bits of the completion word have names. These are APARA_COMPLETION_VALID, APARA_ERROR_HALT, APARA_ERROR_EXCEPTION, APARA_ERROR_RAS, and APARA_ERROR_CODE(word, slot) for a slot's exception code. A thread that ended with $halt reports APARA_COMPLETION_VALID | APARA_ERROR_HALT. The header also defines APARA_DMEM_BASE, the address of DMEM's window.

docs.title: Setting up and running the engine
docs.text: This section gives the protocol that a SPARC program follows to use the engine, and what is allowed at each step. Each step has a test in validation/sparc_apara/, named in brackets. The tests are described in APARA Validation Suite.

docs.title: At power-up
docs.text: No engine thread runs, and IMEM, DMEM and every register of every thread are zero (setup/cold_state). The engine's cycle counter runs from power-up. Nothing needs to be initialized before the first command.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. Load the program into IMEM, one word at a time, through the control unit, with apara_load_program(words, n). IMEM is shared by the four threads, so one program image serves all of them, and each thread starts at its own label. apara_read_imem reads a word back (setup/load_verify checks a whole image).

  2. Put the input data in DMEM, in one of two ways:

    • Directly, through the DMEM window, one 32-bit word at a time, with apara_dmem_write_word. This is simple, but each word is a bus access by the SPARC.
    • By DMA, which copies from main memory while the SPARC goes on with other work. apara_dma_load copies and waits. apara_dma_start and apara_dma_wait let the SPARC overlap several copies, or do its own work in the meantime. A copy can also gather strided data.

    An engine program compiled from C may also need its initialized globals, which apara_load_dmem_image writes (see Carrying the engine's program).

  3. Set each thread's registers, its arguments, with apara_write_thread_register, and start it at an IMEM address, with apara_start_thread. Threads may be started one after another, or at different times (threads/staggered).

  4. Learn that the thread has stopped, by polling or by an interrupt (see Polling or an interrupt). The completion word says how the thread stopped. A thread that ended with $halt reports APARA_COMPLETION_VALID | APARA_ERROR_HALT. After an exception, the word has APARA_ERROR_EXCEPTION and each slot's exception code (APARA_ERROR_CODE(word, slot)), and apara_thread_stop_pc gives the bundle that failed.
  5. Collect the results from DMEM, either directly, with apara_dmem_read_word and apara_dmem_read_dword, or by DMA to main memory, with apara_dma_store.
  6. Start again, for the next piece of work. A thread that stopped with $halt can be started again at once, with new registers. A thread stopped by an exception must first be reset with apara_reset_thread, which clears its PC, return-address stack and ERROR, and keeps its registers (interference/fault_isolation). A new program may be loaded over the old one between runs (setup/reload_program).

setup/offload_poll and setup/offload_interrupt carry out all six steps for an engine program compiled from C.

docs.title: Polling or an interrupt
docs.text:
• Polling. apara_poll_thread(t) returns 0 while the thread runs, and its completion word once it has stopped. apara_wait_thread(t) polls until then. Each poll is a control-unit command, which takes several bus accesses. Polling is the simplest choice for a SPARC program that has nothing else to do while it waits.
  • An interrupt. apara_request_completion_interrupt(t) asks the control unit to raise the engine's interrupt when thread t stops. The SPARC goes on with its own work. Its interrupt handler reads the completion word with apara_thread_completion, and clears the interrupt with apara_clear_interrupt.

A program that takes interrupts is linked with the interrupt startup code, compiler/crt0_interrupts.s. It registers its handler with the dispatch routines of compiler/include/ajit_mt_irc.h (see Taking interrupts), and enables IRL 14 in the Interrupt Controller. The following lines are from validation/sparc_apara/basic/run_interrupt/:

void engine_handler(void)
{
    completion = apara_thread_completion(0);   // the stop, as apara_poll_thread() would report it
    apara_clear_interrupt(0);                  // clear the source
}

int main(void)
{
    ajit_initialize_interrupt_handlers_to_null();
    ajit_set_interrupt_handler(EXTERNAL_IRL, engine_handler);
    writeInterruptControlRegister(0, 0, (1u << EXTERNAL_IRL) | 1u);   // slot 0: enable, IRL 14

    apara_load_program(kernel_program, KERNEL_PROGRAM_WORDS);
    apara_start_thread(0, KERNEL_LOOP);
    apara_request_completion_interrupt(0);
    ...                                        // the SPARC goes on with its own work
}

In the validation suite, the line STARTUP = crt0_interrupts.s in the test's .vprj selects the interrupt startup code. Outside the suite, the environment variable CRT0 does the same:

CRT0=crt0_interrupts.s $SPARC_HOME/compiler/compile_c.sh my_program.c

Either way, each stop is reported exactly once. After a poll has returned a thread's stop, the next poll returns 0 until the thread has been started and has stopped again (threads/staggered). A program that polls several threads can therefore poll them in any order, and never counts one stop twice.

docs.title: What may happen while threads run
docs.text:
• Each thread on its own data. Threads do not disturb one another as long as each writes only its own part of DMEM (interference/disjoint_regions). One thread's exception stops only that thread (interference/fault_isolation).
  • The SPARC and the DMA unit may read and write other parts of DMEM while threads run, and may watch a running thread's progress word (interference/host_while_running, interference/dma_while_running).
  • Not while running. Loading IMEM, or writing a running thread's registers, is not allowed while the thread runs. The control unit carries out such commands, but when they take effect in the running thread is undefined. The SPARC program should wait for the thread to stop first, or stop it with apara_reset_thread.

docs.title: Threads sharing data
docs.text: The engine's instruction set has no atomic read-modify-write. Threads that update the same DMEM word with a load, an add and a store therefore race. Another thread's update can fall between one thread's load and its store, and is then lost. The test interference/shared_counter shows this. In it, four threads each add 1 to one word, 1000 times, and the word ends below 4000. Threads should therefore work on their own data, and leave the SPARC to combine their results, as linalg/dot_threads does with four partial dot products.

docs.title: The SPARC's data cache
docs.text: The engine's windows are never cached, and the routines reach them with MMU-bypass accesses. Main memory may be cached, in the pages that the MMU marks cacheable, and the caches do not see the engine's writes. After the DMA unit, or an engine program, writes main memory, the SPARC should read that data straight from memory with an MMU-bypass load (the tests' physical_word), or flush its data cache first (see Model Components).

docs.title: Floating point on the SPARC side
docs.text: The SPARC's startup code (compiler/crt0.s) leaves the FPU off. A SPARC program that computes with floats, for example to check an engine's float results, turns the FPU on first, by setting the PSR's EF bit. The helper enable_fpu in validation/sparc_apara/apara_common.h does this (linalg/saxpy).

docs.title: Carrying the engine's program
docs.text:
compiler/apara/apara_obj_to_c.py assembles an engine program and writes it as a C header:

python3 $SPARC_HOME/compiler/apara/apara_obj_to_c.py kernel.mcode      # writes kernel.mcode.h

static const uint32_t kernel_program[] = { ... };   // IMEM words 0, 1, ...
#define KERNEL_PROGRAM_WORDS 33
#define KERNEL_START 0x0                             // each label's address

The names come from the file name, and the option --name chooses another.

An engine program written in C (see The C Compiler) is handled in the same way. apara_obj_to_c.py kernel.c compiles it for the system, with DMEM at its window address, and writes kernel.c.h. That header also gives each global variable's DMEM byte offset, and the DMEM words that its initializers set:

#define KERNEL_DMEM_DATA 0x0                              // each global's DMEM offset
static const uint32_t kernel_dmem_image[] = { ... };     // (offset, value) pairs
#define KERNEL_DMEM_IMAGE_WORDS 6

The SPARC program then loads the program and the initial data, puts its input at the globals' offsets, and reads the results from them:

apara_load_program(kernel_program, KERNEL_PROGRAM_WORDS);
apara_load_dmem_image(kernel_dmem_image, KERNEL_DMEM_IMAGE_WORDS);
apara_dma_load(0, KERNEL_DMEM_DATA, (uint32_t) data, sizeof(data));

The parameters of an __entry function arrive in $r1, $r2, and so on, which are set with apara_write_thread_register before the thread starts. The image holds only the non-zero words. DMEM keeps whatever an earlier program left in it, so the SPARC program clears any globals that must start at zero, unless this is the first program since power-up. The test setup/offload_poll is a complete example. Its engine program, vector_stats.c, computes the sum, minimum and maximum of 64 values.

docs.title: Writing a new program
docs.text:
This section needs the cross-toolchain (step 4 of Installation), and the sparc_apara models built as in Run it.

This section builds a new program from scratch. The SPARC program offloads a vector addition, Z = X + Y on 32 int16 elements, to the engine, and checks the engine's result. Its two source files are in $SPARC_HOME/docs/source/examples/apara_vadd/. They can be typed in from this page, or copied from there.

docs.title: 1. Make a working folder
docs.text:
The following commands create a working folder outside the repository, and copy the two source files into it:

mkdir -p ~/apara_programs/my_vadd
cd ~/apara_programs/my_vadd
cp $SPARC_HOME/docs/source/examples/apara_vadd/vadd.mcode .
cp $SPARC_HOME/docs/source/examples/apara_vadd/my_vadd.c .

docs.title: 2. Write the engine program
docs.text:
The engine program, vadd.mcode, is the following:

// vadd.mcode: Z = X + Y on 32 int16 elements, 16 elements per loop pass.
// $r9 holds the address of DMEM's window, set by the SPARC.
// X is at DMEM offset 0, Y at offset 64, and Z at offset 128.

start:
    || + $r20 ($i64) $r9 0  + $r22 ($i64) $r0 1 ;     // $r20 walks the arrays, 2 passes
loop:
    || $ld ($u256) $r1 [$r20 + 0]  $ld ($u256) $r5 [$r20 + 64] ;
    || $v + $r11 ($vi16) $r1 $r5   $v + $r12 ($vi16) $r2 $r6
       $v + $r13 ($vi16) $r3 $r7   $v + $r14 ($vi16) $r4 $r8 ;
    || $st ($u256) [$r20 + 128] $r11  + $r20 ($i64) $r20 32 ;
    || ? ($i64) $r22 > --1 $goto loop ;
    || $halt ;

The SPARC program places X at DMEM offset 0 and Y at offset 64, and passes DMEM's window address in $r9. The program works as follows:

  1. The first bundle sets $r20 to the start of the arrays, and the loop counter $r22 to 1, for two passes.
  2. In each pass, the first bundle of the loop loads 16 elements of X into $r1 to $r4, and 16 elements of Y into $r5 to $r8. Each ($u256) load reads 256 bits, which is four registers.
  3. The next bundle adds them with four vector adds. Each $v + with the type ($vi16) adds four pairs of 16-bit elements.
  4. The third bundle stores the 16 sums at $r20 + 128, in Z, and moves $r20 on by 32 bytes. Both instructions read the old value of $r20, because all instructions of a bundle read their registers before any of them writes.
  5. The branch counts $r22 down, and goes back to loop while it is above zero. After two passes the thread reaches $halt.

docs.title: 3. Turn it into a C header
docs.text:
The following command assembles the engine program, and writes it as a C header:

python3 $SPARC_HOME/compiler/apara/apara_obj_to_c.py vadd.mcode

The header, vadd.mcode.h, holds the program as the array vadd_program[], its size, and the address of each label:

#define VADD_PROGRAM_WORDS 41

#define VADD_START 0x0
#define VADD_LOOP 0x8

The header must be written again after every change to vadd.mcode.

docs.title: 4. Write the SPARC program
docs.text:
The SPARC program, my_vadd.c, is the following:

// my_vadd.c: the SPARC offloads Z = X + Y, on 32 int16 elements, to the
// APARA engine, and checks the engine's result.

#include "apara_access_routines.h"
#include "vadd.mcode.h"

#define N 32
int16_t x[N] __attribute__((aligned(8)));
int16_t y[N] __attribute__((aligned(8)));

int main(void)
{
    uint32_t pass = 1;
    int i;

    for (i = 0; i < N; i++)
    {
        x[i] = (int16_t) (100 * i - 1000);
        y[i] = (int16_t) (7 * i);
    }

    apara_load_program(vadd_program, VADD_PROGRAM_WORDS);    // the engine's program
    apara_dma_load(0, 0, (uint32_t) x, sizeof(x));            // x -> DMEM offset 0
    apara_dma_load(1, 64, (uint32_t) y, sizeof(y));           // y -> DMEM offset 64

    apara_write_thread_register(0, 9, APARA_DMEM_BASE);      // $r9 = DMEM's window
    apara_start_thread(0, VADD_START);
    if (apara_wait_thread(0) != (APARA_COMPLETION_VALID | APARA_ERROR_HALT))
        pass = 0;

    // Z, at DMEM offset 128: two int16 elements in each 32-bit word.
    for (i = 0; i < N; i += 2)
    {
        uint32_t w = apara_dmem_read_word(128 + 2 * i);
        int16_t z0 = (int16_t) (w >> 16), z1 = (int16_t) w;
        if (z0 != (int16_t) (x[i] + y[i]) || z1 != (int16_t) (x[i + 1] + y[i + 1]))
            pass = 0;
    }

    // Report pass (1) or fail (0) in %o0, and halt.
    __asm__ __volatile__("mov %0, %%o0\n\tta 0" : : "r"(pass) : "o0");
    while (1) {}
    return 0;
}

It takes the same steps as the dot product example. It loads the program, copies X and Y into DMEM by DMA, passes DMEM's window address in $r9, starts thread 0 at VADD_START, and waits for the thread to stop. This time it reads the results directly from DMEM, with apara_dmem_read_word. Each 32-bit word of DMEM holds two int16 elements, and the first element is in the upper half, because DMEM is big-endian like the SPARC. The program then reports pass (1) or fail (0) in %o0, and halts with ta 0.

docs.title: 5. Compile it
docs.text:
The following command compiles the SPARC program into a memory image:

$SPARC_HOME/compiler/compile_c.sh my_vadd.c

It writes my_vadd.hex, and the disassembly my_vadd.objdump. It may warn that the section .data does not exist. The warning is expected, because the program has no initialized data.

docs.title: 6. Run it
docs.text:
The following command runs the memory image on the C++ model:

$SPARC_HOME/model/system_models/sparc_apara/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_sparc_apara my_vadd.hex

PROCESSOR STATE: ERROR
...
o0 0x1
...
Simulation halted after 11587 cycles.

%o0 is 1, so every element of Z was right. The Sitar model gives the same result, in 73590 clock cycles:

$SPARC_HOME/model/system_models/sparc_apara/sitar_model/executable/sparc_sim_sitar_sparc_apara my_vadd.hex

As in Getting Started, an expected-results file makes the simulator check the result itself. The following commands write one, with the single line REG o0 0x1 0xffffffff, and run the check:

echo "REG o0 0x1 0xffffffff" > my_vadd.expected
$SPARC_HOME/model/system_models/sparc_apara/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_sparc_apara my_vadd.hex my_vadd.expected

PASS: o0 = 0x1
OVERALL: PASS (1 checks)

docs.title: 7. Try a change
docs.text:
To see a failure, change the first $v + in vadd.mcode to $v -, so that four of the 32 elements are subtracted instead of added. Then write the header again, compile, and run:

python3 $SPARC_HOME/compiler/apara/apara_obj_to_c.py vadd.mcode
$SPARC_HOME/compiler/compile_c.sh my_vadd.c
$SPARC_HOME/model/system_models/sparc_apara/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_sparc_apara my_vadd.hex my_vadd.expected

The SPARC program's check now fails, so %o0 is 0, and the run reports the failure:

FAIL: o0 expected 0x1 (mask 0xffffffff) got 0x0
OVERALL: FAIL (1 checks)

Change the instruction back, and write the header again, before going on.

docs.title: 8. Make it a test
docs.text:
A .vprj file turns the program into a test, which the validation runner builds and runs. The file my_vadd.vprj names the SPARC program and its engine program, and the expected result:

SOURCES = my_vadd.c
MCODE = vadd.mcode

RESULTS =
o0=0x00000001

The line MCODE = vadd.mcode makes the build script write vadd.mcode.h before it compiles the SPARC program. The following commands copy the file, build the test, and run it on the C++ model of sparc_apara:

cp $SPARC_HOME/docs/source/examples/apara_vadd/my_vadd.vprj .
cd $SPARC_HOME
python3 validation/build_hex.py ~/apara_programs/my_vadd
python3 validation/run_tests.py ~/apara_programs/my_vadd --config sparc_apara

[PASS] .../my_vadd/my_vadd.vprj

1/1 tests passed

The option --sitar runs it on the Sitar model instead. APARA Validation Suite describes the format of the tests, and how to add a test to the suite itself.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
The tests in validation/sparc_apara/ are worked examples of the next steps. Each one is a SPARC program with its engine programs, and can be copied and changed in the same way as my_vadd.

To learn Start from Running one program on four threads, each on its own part of the data threads/threads_4 Writing the engine program in C setup/offload_poll, with vector_stats.c Learning of a stop by interrupt basic/run_interrupt, and setup/offload_interrupt Gathering strided data with one DMA copy basic/dma_interrupt An exception in an engine thread, and recovering from it basic/exception, and interference/fault_isolation A larger kernel, a matrix product on four threads linalg/matmul

On the Sitar model, --stats shows where the engine's time went, for example in register-lock stalls or DMEM bank conflicts. The counters are described in APARA Timing Model.

docs.title: APARA Timing Model
docs.text:
The sitar_model of the apara configuration is a cycle-level model of the engine's pipeline, following the APARA microarchitecture document, and is the same pipeline sparc_apara uses.

As everywhere in this project, the model keeps function and timing apart. What each bundle does comes from the same C++ class the fast functional model runs, so the two models always compute the same results. The timing comes from the Sitar structure itself: the pipeline's stages are modules, the channels between them are nets, and a bundle's time is spent actually waiting in them, for a free channel, a register, or the divider. It is never computed after the fact. This is what makes the timing model trustworthy for experiments: change a channel depth or a latency, and every effect it has on the rest of the pipeline follows by itself.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
The engine's five stages, each a module, are joined by nets with the hardware's channel depths: 2 entries, except 1 for EXEC's results and for WRITEBACK's notices to FETCH. Each module takes its inputs in the first half of a cycle and sends its outputs in the second half, so a bundle spends at least one cycle in each stage. A stage whose output channel is full holds its bundle until there is room, and the stages before it then fill up and wait too. This is the hardware's elastic pipeline.

  • FETCH Picks a running thread (round robin), reads the 8-word IMEM line holding its PC, and sends that line's bundles to DECODE, one per cycle and in PC order, before picking another thread. It predicts each bundle's next PC with the branch target buffer (BTB).
  • DECODE Decodes a bundle: which registers it reads and writes, how long it will take in EXEC, and whether it needs the divider. It then sends the bundle on to REGFILE, on its thread's own channel.
  • REGFILE Holds one waiting bundle per thread. Each cycle it issues one of them (round robin) whose registers are all free, provided a token is free, and locks the registers that bundle will write. When the bundle's result comes back from EXEC, it releases those locks and the token.
  • EXEC Executes the bundle, then holds it for its latency. EXEC owns the engine's state: its memories, registers, and threads. It skips bundles fetched on a wrong path.
  • WRITEBACK Retires the bundle. It sends FETCH a PC correction when a bundle's next PC was mispredicted, and a notice when a thread has stopped.

docs.title: A bundle's journey
docs.text: A bundle with no stalls is fetched in some cycle c, decoded in c+1, issued by REGFILE in c+2, and executed in EXEC from c+3. Its result comes back to REGFILE after its latency, and it leaves WRITEBACK one cycle later. So a program of one 1-cycle bundle takes 6 cycles from start to finish. Later bundles overlap with it, so a stream of independent bundles completes at one bundle per cycle.

docs.title: Modules and nets
docs.text:
The apara configuration's Top holds one AparaEngine and nothing else: there is no SPARC core and no system around it. This shows which design unit instantiates which, and the nets joining the stages.

Top
 |
 +-- engine : AparaEngine (module)
      |
      +-- fetch     : AparaFetch (module)
      |
      +-- decode    : AparaDecode (module)
      |
      +-- regfile   : AparaRegfile (module)
      |
      +-- exec      : AparaExec (module)
      |
      +-- writeback : AparaWriteback (module)

fetch.toDecode          --fetchToDecode-->          decode.fromFetch
decode.toRegfile[0..3]  --decodeToRegfile[0..3]-->  regfile.fromDecode[0..3]
regfile.toExec          --regfileToExec-->          exec.fromRegfile
exec.toRegfile          --execToRegfile-->          regfile.fromExec
regfile.toWriteback     --regfileToWriteback-->     writeback.fromRegfile
writeback.correctionOut --correctionNet-->          fetch.correctionIn
writeback.haltOut       --haltNet-->                fetch.haltIn
exec.fetchControlOut    --fetchControlNet-->        fetch.controlIn

decodeToRegfile is one net per thread, so REGFILE can hold a waiting bundle of each thread and issue whichever one is ready. fetchControlNet carries thread starts and resets to FETCH.

docs.title: Instruction latency
docs.text:
A bundle's time in EXEC is the latency of its slowest instruction, or the time of its memory accesses if that is longer. The latencies come from a table, by instruction class. The defaults:

Entry Cycles Covers nop any, control any, halt any, misc any, logic any 1 $null, branches/calls/returns, $halt, $set $slice $pack, | & ^ ~| ~& ~^ arith int<=32, arith fp<=16 1 + - *, scalar and vector arith int64 2 arith fp32, arith fp64 3 shift int<=32 / shift int64 1 / 2 << >> dot int<=32, dot fp<=16 / dot int64, dot fp32, dot fp64 2 / 3 cast narrow / cast wide 1 / 2 narrow: integer to integer, float to integer, floats up to f16 vreduce any 2 assumed: not in the hardware's table cmov any 1 assumed: not in the hardware's table memory local 3 a bundle's DMEM accesses divide any, sqrt any 10 the designer's figure, to be confirmed

To try other latencies, pass --latency-file <file> to the apara simulator. Each line of the file overrides one entry, as <class> <operands> <cycles>, and # starts a comment:

arith fp32 5     # an f32 add/subtract/multiply takes 5 cycles
divide any 20

docs.title: Data memory
docs.text: DMEM has two banks (address bit 15 selects the bank), each with its own 256-bit port. A bundle's accesses to different banks proceed in parallel. Accesses to the same bank go one after another, each extra one adding a cycle (the bankConflictCycles knob). Placing two arrays that are read together in different banks avoids the conflict.

docs.title: The divider
docs.text: Integer and float divides and square roots share one divider. A bundle that needs it waits in EXEC until the previous user has finished.

docs.title: EXEC
docs.text: By default EXEC is internally pipelined: it takes a new bundle every cycle, and results leave it in order, one per cycle. The pipelined knob selects instead a stage that holds one bundle for its whole latency.

docs.title: Register locks and tokens
docs.text:
A bundle waits in REGFILE while any register it reads or writes is locked by an earlier bundle of its thread, that is, until the earlier bundle's result is back. This is how the pipeline keeps a thread's bundles in order without stalling the other threads.

At most 2 bundles are in EXEC at a time, one per REGFILE token. A token comes back with the bundle's result, two cycles after issue for a 1-cycle bundle, so two tokens are exactly enough to issue one bundle every cycle.

docs.title: Branch prediction
docs.text:
The branch target buffer has 256 entries, direct mapped by the low 8 bits of a bundle's PC, and shared by the four threads. Each entry holds a 22-bit tag, a 2-bit counter (0 strongly taken, 3 strongly not taken), and a target. A lookup predicts the entry's target if the tag matches and the counter is below 3, and otherwise the next bundle.

Only PC corrections train the BTB: a correction to a taken branch lowers the counter and sets the target, one to a not-taken branch raises the counter, and a new entry starts at 0 or 3 accordingly.

Calls and returns are predicted the same way, by their BTB entry: a $return is predicted to go where it went last time. Some consequences for programs, each measured by a test in validation/apara/predictor/:

  • A loop's closing branch mispredicts once per run of the loop, at its exit, once the BTB has learned it.
  • A correctly predicted branch never trains its entry. So a loop that is entered again and again (an inner loop) pulls its counter up by one at each exit, and after three exits the entry predicts "not taken": from then on every run of the inner loop mispredicts twice, at its first pass and at its exit (nested_loops).
  • A function called from several places mispredicts its return whenever the caller changes (call_sites).
  • Two branches whose PCs share their low 8 bits share an entry, and evict each other (alias).

docs.title: Mispredicts
docs.text: EXEC compares each bundle's actual next PC with the one FETCH predicted. On a mismatch, the thread's following bundles, already fetched on the wrong path, are skipped (not executed, though their register locks are still released) until FETCH, corrected by WRITEBACK, sends the first bundle of the right path. With one thread, a mispredict costs 5 cycles. With several, the other threads keep the pipeline busy meanwhile. A thread's halting bundle is handled the same way, except that the thread then stays stopped.

docs.title: Knobs
docs.text:
All the timing knobs are set in one place, Top.sitar in apara (model/system_models/apara/sitar_model/src/Top.sitar) and System.sitar in sparc_apara. Rebuild after a change.

Knob Default Meaning engine.fetch.imemDelay 0 Cycles between FETCH picking a thread and its IMEM line arriving. engine.exec.pipelined true false: EXEC holds one bundle for its whole latency. engine.exec.latency.bankConflictCycles 1 Cycles per extra same-bank access in a bundle. engine.regfile.tokens 2 How many bundles may be in EXEC at once. engine.regfile.interlock true false: REGFILE ignores its register locks, to show which reads would be hazards without them (see Hazards). Not a hardware option.

--stats prints the pipeline's counters: bundles fetched, executed, and skipped, mispredicts, fetches that followed a BTB prediction, the cycles lost to register locks, to tokens, and to the divider, bank conflicts, and the two hazard checks (see Performance Modeling).

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The timing model is checked by three suites in validation/apara/, each count derived by hand from the rules above, and written in the test's header:

  • timing/, microbenchmarks with exact cycle counts: one bundle (6 cycles), a stream of bundles at full rate, latency, a read-after-write stall against the independent case, the shared divider, a bank conflict against the same accesses on two banks, a mispredict, and two threads sharing the pipeline.
  • predictor/, exact mispredict counts for loops, nested loops, aliasing entries, and calls and returns.
  • hazards/, the register interlock (see Hazards).

run_tests.py --sitar checks every count exactly. The counts are derived for the default knob values and latency table, so the suite checks the timing model at those settings only. Each knob was also checked by setting it to several values, one at a time: every count moved by exactly the amount the rules predict. timing/README.md has those counts, and how to set the knobs back to their defaults afterwards.

The kernels and C programs of the other suites run on the timing model too, and their --stats show where a larger program spends its cycles. For example, an 8x8 matrix product (kernels/matmul_i8) takes 122 cycles on one thread and 112 on four: its memory-heavy bundles stay in EXEC 3 cycles or more, so the two REGFILE tokens, not the threads, limit its throughput.

The open items, such as the latencies marked above, EXEC's structure, and the order of same-bank accesses, are listed in Deviations and Findings.

docs.title: APARA Validation Suite
docs.text:
The APARA engine has two sets of tests. The engine suites test the engine on its own, in the apara configuration. The system suites test a SPARC program using the engine, in the sparc_apara configuration. This page describes what each set contains, how to run it on both models, and how to add a test. The general format of the SPARC tests, and the runner validation/run_tests.py, are described in Validation Suite.

Set Folder Configuration Runner Tests Engine suites validation/apara/ apara validation/apara/run_tests.py 108 System suites validation/sparc_apara/ sparc_apara validation/run_tests.py --config sparc_apara 26

The commands on this page use $SPARC_HOME, the repository's folder, as set in step 2 of Installation.

docs.title: Before running the tests
docs.text:
Each runner runs the plain build of its configuration's models. The following commands build the C++ model and the Sitar model of both configurations:

cd $SPARC_HOME/model/system_models/apara/cpp_model
./build.sh
cd $SPARC_HOME/model/system_models/apara/sitar_model
./build.sh
cd $SPARC_HOME/model/system_models/sparc_apara/cpp_model
./build.sh
cd $SPARC_HOME/model/system_models/sparc_apara/sitar_model
./build.sh

The Sitar models need Sitar (step 3 of Installation). The executables of apara are executable/apara_sim_cpp and executable/apara_sim_sitar, and those of sparc_apara are executable/sparc_sim_cpp_sparc_apara and executable/sparc_sim_sitar_sparc_apara.

No cross-toolchain is needed to run the tests. The engine suites are assembled by the runner itself, with the engine's assembler, which is a Python program. The system suites' memory images are already built and committed. The cross-toolchain is needed only to rebuild a system test after a change to its sources (see Rebuilding the memory images).

docs.title: What they contain
docs.text:
validation/apara/ holds the engine's own test suites, one folder each:

Folder Tests What they check isa/ 29 Every instruction, in one subfolder per class (alu_int, alu_float, vector, cast, bits, cmov, memory, control). The tests cover each operation on each type, edge values (wraparound, sign extension, rounding), immediates and increments at their limits, and every exception. sequences/ 7 Instructions working together. Examples are full 8-slot bundles, loops, a recurrence in one bundle per step, a block copy with auto-increments, threads sharing DMEM, and one thread's fault not stopping the others. hazards/ 10 The pipeline's handling of dependences between bundles (see Hazards). predictor/ 6 The branch predictor, with loops, nested loops, two branches sharing a predictor entry, and calls and returns. Each test's mispredict count is derived from the predictor's rules. asm_errors/ 21 Programs the assembler must reject. Examples are a register written twice in a bundle (also through multi-register writes and increments), too many control transfers, divides or memory operations in a bundle, values out of range, and invalid types. timing/ 10 Microbenchmarks with exact cycle counts, derived by hand from the timing rules. Its README.md also has each test's counts for other settings of the knobs. kernels/ 6 Larger hand-scheduled programs. These are a dot product, a vector addition, SAXPY, a reduction, and matrix products on one and four threads. c_programs/ 11 Programs compiled from C with the C compiler. They cover the language's features, sorting, a prime sieve, and linear algebra. deviations/ 8 Behavior where the model departs, on purpose, from the engine's reference model (see Deviations and Findings).

Each folder has a README.md describing its tests. A good way to learn the instruction set is to read the tests of isa/ next to the Instruction Set, and then the programs of kernels/.

docs.title: A test
docs.text:
A test is a source file and a .vprj file of the same name. The .vprj says how to run the program and what to expect, in the same spirit as the SPARC tests. For example, the timing test timing/t3_latency is the following program:

// Timing: EXEC latency. An f32 add takes 3 cycles in EXEC (cycles 3-5).
// The $halt behind it enters EXEC in cycle 4 but results leave in order,
// one per cycle: the add's in cycle 5, the halt's in 6; WRITEBACK in 8:
// 9 cycles.
//
    || + $r1 ($f32) $r2 $r3 ;
    || $halt ;

Its .vprj gives the exact cycle count that the timing model must reach:

SOURCES = t3_latency.mcode
CYCLES = 9

RESULTS =

The source's header explains where the expected count comes from. A functional test sets registers and memory in INIT, and lists the expected results in RESULTS. The following lines are from isa/control/control.vprj:

SOURCES = control.mcode

INIT =
r1 = 5
r3 = 0xbfc00000

RESULTS =
r1 = 0xffffffffffffffff
r2 = 0xf

The lines of INIT and RESULTS have the following forms:

Line Meaning r3 = 0x10 Thread 0's $r3. t1.r3 = 0x10 Thread 1's $r3. m[0x80] = 0x0102030405060708 The DMEM dword (8 bytes) at byte address 0x80. m[C+0x8] = 0x2f2 In a C test, a dword of the global C. t1.pc = 0x9 (RESULTS only) Where thread 1 stopped. error = 0x2000000 (RESULTS only) Thread 0's ERROR register. The value 0x2000000 is a $halt.

A value in RESULTS may be followed by a mask, which selects the bits that are compared.

The other keys are the following:

Key Meaning SOURCES = prog.mcode The program. It may be mcode, C (.c, compiled first), or an object file (.obj). THREADS = 0x0 worker Start a thread at each of these IMEM addresses or labels. The default is one thread at 0x0. CYCLES = 12 The exact cycle count on the timing model, with the default timing settings. MISPREDICTS = 2, BTB_PREDICTIONS = 3 The exact branch predictor counts on the timing model. HAZARDS_UNLOCKED = 1 The hazards that the timing model must count when built without the interlock (see Hazards). ASM_ERROR = written twice The program must not assemble, and the error message must contain this text. DEVIATION = <why> The test depends on one of the model's deviations. MAX_CYCLES = 100000 A larger limit, for a long test. APCC_FLAGS = -O0 Options for the C compiler.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
The engine suites have their own runner, validation/apara/run_tests.py. The following commands run every suite, first on the C++ model and then on the Sitar model:

cd $SPARC_HOME
python3 validation/apara/run_tests.py
python3 validation/apara/run_tests.py --sitar

For each test, the runner assembles or compiles the program, writes its files into validation/apara/build/<test>/, runs it, and prints PASS or FAIL. It then prints a summary for each suite:

PASS  timing/t1_halt.vprj
...
  asm_errors     21/21 passed
  c_programs     11/11 passed
  deviations     8/8 passed
  hazards        10/10 passed
  isa            29/29 passed
  kernels        6/6 passed
  predictor      6/6 passed
  sequences      7/7 passed
  timing         10/10 passed
OVERALL: 108 passed, 0 failed

With --sitar, the runner also checks the timing keys CYCLES, MISPREDICTS, BTB_PREDICTIONS and HAZARDS_UNLOCKED. The runner can also be given one suite, or one .vprj:

cd $SPARC_HOME
python3 validation/apara/run_tests.py validation/apara/hazards --sitar
python3 validation/apara/run_tests.py validation/apara/timing/t3_latency.vprj --sitar

A failing test can be run again by hand, with the files the runner left in validation/apara/build/<test>/, and the options of Running a program, such as --trace.

docs.title: Adding a test
docs.text: To add a test, write a source file and its .vprj in a suite's folder, and run the suite. Nothing needs to be registered, because the runner finds every .vprj file in the folders it is given. To find the expected values of a new test, run it once with --dump-results - (see Running a program). Then check every value by hand, or with an independent calculation, before writing it down.

docs.title: What they contain
docs.text:
validation/sparc_apara/ holds the tests of the SPARC using the engine. Each test is a bare-metal SPARC C program, with one or more engine programs. The tests are grouped in five folders:

Folder Tests What they check basic/ 8 Each part of the engine's interface on its own. The tests cover IMEM and registers, running and polling, the completion interrupt, exceptions, four threads, the engine's own main-memory accesses, DMA and its interrupt, and a whole offload by DMA (dma_dot_product). setup/ 5 Bringing the engine up, with one thread. The tests cover its state at power-up, loading and reading back its memories, complete offloads of a program compiled from C (by polling and by interrupt), and loading a second program over the first. threads/ 5 The same program on 1, 2, 3 and 4 threads, each on its own slice of the data, and threads started and restarted at different times. interference/ 5 Whether threads, the SPARC and the DMA unit disturb one another (see What may happen while threads run), and the one real interference, a race on shared data. linalg/ 3 Linear algebra offloaded to the engine. The tests are an 8x8 matrix product on four threads, SAXPY in floating point, and a four-thread dot product compiled from C.

Each folder has a README.md describing its tests, and validation/sparc_apara/README.md summarizes the protocol of Setting up and running the engine. The tests also serve as worked examples for new programs, as listed in Going further.

docs.title: A test
docs.text:
A system test is a folder with a SPARC C program, its engine programs, and a .vprj file. The folder basic/dma_dot_product/ holds the following sources:

File What dma_dot_product.c The SPARC program. kernel.mcode The engine program. dma_dot_product.vprj How to build the test, and what to expect.

Its .vprj names the SPARC program, its engine program, and the expected registers:

SOURCES = dma_dot_product.c
MCODE = kernel.mcode


RESULTS =
o0=0x00000001
o1=0x0000000f

The line MCODE = kernel.mcode names an engine program. The build script writes its C header, kernel.mcode.h, before it compiles the SPARC program. A test may have several MCODE lines, and an engine program may also be written in C (MCODE = kernel.c). The line STARTUP = crt0_interrupts.s links the interrupt startup code, for a test that takes the engine's interrupt. The other files in the folder, such as dma_dot_product.hex and kernel.mcode.h, are written by the build, and are committed so that the tests run without a cross-toolchain.

Every test reports in the same way as the device tests. %o0 is 1 if every check passed, and %o1 has one bit per check. The checks are listed in the header comment of the test's C file. The SPARC program computes the expected results itself.

The tests share some helpers, in validation/sparc_apara/apara_common.h:
