Helper Does report_and_halt(ok, n) Writes 1 to %o0 if all n checks passed, and 0 otherwise, writes ok to %o1, and halts. physical_word(p) Reads a word of main memory with an MMU-bypass load, past the data cache, for data that the engine has written there. dword_equals(o, v) Whether the 64-bit word at DMEM offset o equals the 32-bit value v, sign-extended. next_random(&state) The next number of a fixed pseudo-random sequence, for test data. enable_fpu() Turns on the SPARC's FPU, which the startup code leaves off. HALTED The completion word of a thread that ended with $halt.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
The system suites run with the general runner, on --config sparc_apara. The Sitar model needs a larger cycle limit than the default:

cd $SPARC_HOME
python3 validation/run_tests.py validation/sparc_apara --config sparc_apara
python3 validation/run_tests.py validation/sparc_apara --config sparc_apara --sitar --max-cycles 50000000

[PASS] validation/sparc_apara/basic/dma_dot_product/dma_dot_product.vprj
...
[PASS] validation/sparc_apara/threads/threads_4/threads_4.vprj

26/26 tests passed

One folder, or one test's folder, can be given instead:

cd $SPARC_HOME
python3 validation/run_tests.py validation/sparc_apara/basic --config sparc_apara
python3 validation/run_tests.py validation/sparc_apara/basic/dma_dot_product --config sparc_apara

A test's memory image can also be run by hand, as in An example: offloading a dot product.

docs.title: Rebuilding the memory images
docs.text:
This section needs the cross-toolchain (step 4 of Installation).

After a change to a test's C program or engine program, the following command rebuilds the memory images of a folder of tests. It writes the engine programs' headers, then compiles each SPARC program:

cd $SPARC_HOME
python3 validation/build_hex.py validation/sparc_apara

The runner then runs the new images. Rebuilt .hex files should be committed together with the changed sources.

docs.title: Adding a test
docs.text:
To add a test, make a new folder in one of the five folders, with the SPARC program, its engine programs, and a .vprj that names them. Then build it and run it:

cd $SPARC_HOME
python3 validation/build_hex.py validation/sparc_apara/basic/my_test
python3 validation/run_tests.py validation/sparc_apara/basic/my_test --config sparc_apara

Writing a new program builds such a test step by step. The file validation/sparc_apara/REQUIRES names the components that these tests need, which are the SPARC core, the devices and the engine. The runner therefore runs a new test in validation/sparc_apara/ only on the sparc_apara configuration (see Which tests run on which configuration).

docs.title: The whole suite on sparc_apara
docs.text:
The sparc_apara configuration also runs the general SPARC tests of validation/, because its SPARC core is the one of core_l1cache_mmu_devices. The following command runs every test that the configuration can run, on the C++ model:

cd $SPARC_HOME
python3 validation/run_tests.py validation --config sparc_apara

skipped 108 test(s) under validation/apara: sparc_apara has no apara_standalone
291/291 tests passed (108 skipped)

The 291 tests are the SPARC tests and the 26 system tests. The runner skips the 108 engine tests of validation/apara/, which only their own runner runs.

docs.title: docs/source/examples/apara_vadd/
docs.text:
The example program of the walkthrough "Writing a new program" in Programming the System. The SPARC program my_vadd.c offloads a vector addition of 32 int16 elements to the APARA engine, whose program is vadd.mcode, and checks the engine's result. my_vadd.vprj turns it into a test for validation/run_tests.py --config sparc_apara.

Only the sources are kept here. The walkthrough copies them into a working folder of its own, and builds them there. This folder is not part of the validation suite.

docs.title: docs/source/examples/array_sum/
docs.text: A frozen copy of validation/C/array_sum/'s source, built once with this repository's own vendored toolchain and committed here alongside its .hex/.objdump/.expected. Used by docs/source/examining_core_state_with_gdb.md's walkthrough -- kept separate from the validation copy so the specific addresses that page cites stay correct regardless of which cross-compiler version a reader has installed. Not part of the validation suite itself; don't add this directory to validation/run_tests.py.

docs.title: docs/source/examples/test_template/
docs.text: An illustrative, generic skeleton, not a real, runnable test: the trap table is deliberately left as a placeholder comment rather than the real 256 entries (copy one from any validation/asm/ test instead). Shown by docs/source/writing_and_running_assembly_programs.md under "Recommended format for a test program" as the shape every test in this repository follows. Not part of the validation suite, don't add this directory to validation/run_tests.py.

docs.title: log_viewer/
docs.text: A lightweight, self-contained, single-file browser tool for viewing SPARC V8 instruction/state traces produced by CoreLogger (model/cpp_common_code/CoreLogger.h) -- used by every configuration's cpp_model and sitar_model, since both drive the same SparcCore and therefore emit the same trace format.

docs.title: What's here
docs.text:
• viewer.html -- the viewer itself. A single HTML file, no build step, no external dependencies (works entirely offline, nothing is fetched from the network). Open it directly in any modern browser.
  • test_simple_ADD.log / test_simple_ADD.objdump -- symlinks to a small sample trace and its matching disassembly, generated from the bundled test_simple_ADD example (see below and ../validation/README.md), so you can explore the viewer without building or running anything first. Named to match, not sim_trace.*, so it's the same file the walkthroughs elsewhere produce, not a differently-named copy.

docs.title: Trace format
docs.text: Tab-separated, one row per architectural event (FETCH, TRAP_RAISED, TRAP_ENTER, MEM_READ, MEM_WRITE, ATOMIC, RESET, ANNUL, HALT, or a generic one-off): seq, time, pc, event, detail, followed by the entire current-window processor state (PSR fields named and in binary, general registers in hex). See CoreLogger.h for exactly what each event logs and why. The viewer only requires seq/time/pc/ event/detail to be present -- any extra columns a future trace source adds are simply ignored, not required.

docs.title: Viewing a trace
docs.text:
1. Build the cpp model with logging enabled, and run a test program: 
    model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/build.sh --logging
model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only_logging \
    validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.hex
    This writes test_simple_ADD.log into the current directory (a trace file is always named after the hex file it ran).
  2. Open log_viewer/viewer.html in a browser (double-click it, or open log_viewer/viewer.html / xdg-open log_viewer/viewer.html).
  3. Click Load trace and pick test_simple_ADD.log; click Load objdump and pick validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.objdump (the matching disassembly, see ../validation/README.md).

docs.title: Example: viewing the bundled test_simple_ADD example
docs.text:
From the repository root:

model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/build.sh --logging
model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only_logging \
    validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.hex
open log_viewer/viewer.html   # or: xdg-open log_viewer/viewer.html

Then in the viewer: Load trace -> test_simple_ADD.log (written into the repository root, since that's where the command above was run from), Load objdump -> validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.objdump.

docs.title: The same, via the sitar model
docs.text:
model/system_models/core_only/sitar_model/build.sh --logging
model/system_models/core_only/sitar_model/executable/sparc_sim_sitar_core_only_logging \
    validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.hex \
    validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.expected

Writes test_simple_ADD.log (sparcThread's trace, directly loadable, same as above) and sitar.log (everything else Sitar logs -- see model/system_models/core_only/sitar_model/README.md) into the current directory.

docs.title: Optional: serve it for auto-loading
docs.text:
If you'd rather not click through file pickers every time, serve the directory containing both files and pass them as URL query parameters -- the viewer fetch()es them automatically on load:

cd log_viewer
python3 -m http.server 8000

then open http://localhost:8000/viewer.html?trace=test_simple_ADD.log (the bundled sample -- the viewer also automatically tries the same basename with a .objdump extension, test_simple_ADD.objdump here). For a freshly generated trace, copy it (and its .objdump) into this directory first, or point ?trace= at a relative path if your server root already covers both files. This only works over http(s), not a plain file:// URL -- browsers block a page from reading another local file just by name.

docs.title: Using the viewer
docs.text:
• Search: field=value (e.g. PC=0x1c, l4=0x3434, T=56) matches a specific column; plain text with no = searches every column for a substring.
  • prev / next: step through search matches only. Use the Up/Down arrow keys to step through the trace row by row regardless of search.
  • Click a row in the Trace panel to select it and see its state. Click a line in Disassembly to jump to the first trace row at that address.
  • The Trace panel's event column is colored by event type (e.g. FETCH amber, EXECUTED green, the two trap events orange, HALT red, RESET purple, memory events blue), so a given kind of row is easy to pick out while scanning.
  • All three panels (Disassembly, Trace, State) are independently resizable -- drag the thin dividers between them.
  • Light/dark theme toggle, top right.

docs.title: The Multicore System
docs.text: The multicore configuration models several SPARC V8 cores that share one main memory and one set of peripheral devices. Each core has its own split L1 instruction and data caches and its own MMU, exactly as in the single-core core_l1cache_mmu_devices configuration. The cores reach memory and the devices over one shared bus, so a program can run on all of them at once and share data through memory. The design follows AJIT's multicore processor wherever that design is known.

docs.title: The system at a glance
docs.text:
• Cores. NUM_CORES cores, 4 by default. Core i has core ID i. It reads 0x50520000 | (i << 8) from ASR29, the same register AJIT software uses to find its own core and thread.
  • Caches and MMU. Each core has its own L1 caches and MMU. The caches are write-through, so main memory always holds every value a core has written.
  • Coherence. A run-time option, --coherent, off by default. When it is off, a core's caches can keep an old copy of a line after another core writes to it, and programs read shared data with uncached loads, or flush their caches first. When it is on, a write removes that line from every other core's caches (see Coherent caches).
  • Atomic instructions. LDSTUB and SWAP are atomic across cores in both models, and a library of locks, barriers and semaphores is built on them.
  • Memory and devices. One main memory and one set of devices (Timer, Serial, Interrupt Controller, Scratch-pad), shared by every core. The Interrupt Controller has a slot for each core and delivers each core its own interrupts.
  • Startup. Every core starts at PC 0 and runs the same program, which reads its core ID to decide what to do.
  • End of a run. A run ends when every core has halted.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
The configuration is being built in stages.

Stage Contents Status 1 The cores, the shared bus, startup of every core, checking each core's results, per-core interrupts Done 2 Atomic LDSTUB and SWAP across cores, and a library of synchronization routines (locks, barriers) Done 3 Write-invalidate cache coherence, the --coherent option Done 4 Shared devices from several cores (a console under a lock, TLB shootdown through IPIs) Done 5 OpenMP programs, with a bare-metal OpenMP runtime Done 6 Context switching and a scheduler on each core Planned 7 Parallel simulation of the sitar_model on several host threads Done, with speedup measurements on a larger host to follow

These pages describe what is done, and grow with each stage.

docs.title: Building and running
docs.text:
Both models are built like any other configuration.

cd model/system_models/multicore/cpp_model   && ./build.sh
cd model/system_models/multicore/sitar_model && ./build.sh

A program then runs on all cores at once.

./executable/sparc_sim_cpp_multicore <program.hex> [expected] [max_cycles] [--stats] \
    [--schedule <spec>] [--run-cores <m>] ...

The other options are those of core_l1cache_mmu_devices (cache sizes, serial and timer options), and they apply to every core.

  • --run-cores <m> runs only cores 0 to m-1. The others never leave reset, and the run does not wait for them. With --run-cores 1, any single-core program runs unchanged. The environment variable SPARC_RUN_CORES does the same.
  • --schedule <spec> (cpp_model only) chooses how the cores' instructions are interleaved. See Execution Model.
  • --threads <n> and --thread-map <list> (sitar_model, built with --openmp) run the simulation on several host threads. See Parallel Simulation.
  • --coherent keeps the caches coherent. SPARC_COHERENT=1 does the same, and --no-coherent overrides it. See Coherent caches.
  • --snoop-filter leaves out repeated invalidates. SPARC_SNOOP_FILTER=1 does the same.
  • --stats prints each core's counters, then the shared memory's and devices' counters. The sitar_model also prints the number of bus transactions each core made.

docs.title: Compile-time knobs
docs.text:
Knob Default Where Description NUM_CORES 4 cpp_model: MulticoreConfig.hsitar_model: System's parameter in System.sitar Number of cores, 1 to 4. The Interrupt Controller has slots for 4 cores.

Every Sitar latency knob of the single-core configuration is also in System.sitar, set the same for every core, along with the bus's own bridge.delay. See Model Configuration Settings.

docs.title: In these pages
docs.text:
• Model Structure and Assumptions shows how each model is built, how the shared bus arbitrates between cores, and where the model makes its own assumptions.
  • Execution Model describes how the cpp_model and the sitar_model run several cores, and why their results can differ for some programs.
  • Programming the Multicore System covers the startup file, the core ID, sharing data with and without coherent caches, locks and other synchronization, interrupts on several cores, and the routines provided.
  • Example Programs walks through a parallel array sum and a parallel matrix multiply.
  • Logging and Debugging covers per-core traces, gdb with several cores, and finding data races.
  • Validation Suite lists the multicore tests and how to run them.
  • Parallel Simulation runs the sitar_model on several host threads, and explains when that is faster.

docs.title: Logging and Debugging
docs.text: The logging and gdb support of the single-core configurations works on the multicore configuration too, with each core logged and debugged on its own. This page covers what changes when there are several cores. See Logging and Examining Core State with GDB for the tools themselves.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
A build with --logging writes a separate instruction trace for each core, so the traces of different cores never interleave.

cd model/system_models/multicore/sitar_model
./build.sh --logging
./executable/sparc_sim_sitar_multicore_logging my_test.hex
File Contents my_test.log Core 0's trace, the same name the single-core configurations use. my_test.core1.log, my_test.core2.log, ... The trace of each other core. sitar.log The sitar_model's own module log, as in the single-core configurations. It records, for example, when each core halts.

Each trace can be opened in the log viewer on its own. The cpp_model writes the same per-core trace files. A parallel run of the sitar_model writes one module log per host thread instead of sitar.log (see Parallel Simulation).

docs.title: Debugging with gdb
docs.text:
A build with --debug supports the commands of debug/sparc.gdb. Every command that concerns one core's state takes a coreid= option. On a breakpoint, leaving it out means any core can trigger it. When reading registers, leaving it out means core 0.

cd model/system_models/multicore/sitar_model
./build.sh --debug
gdb ./executable/sparc_sim_sitar_multicore_debug

(gdb) source ../../../../debug/sparc.gdb
(gdb) sparc-break pc=0x2a40 coreid=2
(gdb) run my_test.hex
(gdb) sparc-print-reg asr29 coreid=2
asr29 = 0x50520200 (1347551744)
(gdb) sparc-print-reg pc coreid=1
(gdb) sparc-break-trap coreid=3
(gdb) continue

ASR29 holds the core ID in bits 15 to 8, so sparc-print-reg asr29 shows at a glance which core a register dump belongs to. Main memory is shared, so the memory commands (sparc-print-mem and the memory watchpoints) see the same memory whichever core is named. The device registers cannot be read or watched from gdb, and sparc-print-mem reports an error for an address outside main memory. See the GDB Command Reference for every command.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text: --stats prints each core's counters (instructions, loads, stores, cache hits and misses, TLB counters) under its own heading, then the counters of main memory and the devices. The sitar_model also prints the number of bus transactions each core made, which shows how much each core used the shared bus.

docs.title: Finding data races
docs.text:
A program whose result depends on the order of the cores' memory accesses has a data race. The cpp_model's scheduling strategies (see Execution Model) are the tool for finding one. A program that gives the same result under several strategies and seeds, and on the sitar_model, is unlikely to depend on the interleaving.

for s in rr:1 rr:4 rr-fixed:1 random:7:32 random:99:3; do
    SPARC_SCHEDULE=$s validation/run_tests.py validation/multicore --config multicore
done

Running with SPARC_ALWAYS_CACHEABLE=1 as well catches programs that read an old cached copy of shared data.

docs.title: Example Programs
docs.text: Two complete programs show the patterns of Programming the Multicore System at work. Both are bare-metal C programs, with no operating system and no runtime library beyond the startup file. A third, on the OpenMP Programs page, does the work of the second with one pragma. All are also tests in the validation suite, in validation/multicore/examples/, so they are known to run on both models, under every cpp scheduling strategy, with the caches in use or not.

docs.title: Parallel array sum
docs.text:
parallel_sum.c sums an array of 4096 words on four cores. The array is split into four slices of 1024 words, and core i fills and sums slice i. Each core then publishes its partial sum, and core 0 adds the four partial sums together.

#define N         4096
#define SLICE     (N / NUM_CORES)

int data[N];
volatile uint32_t partial_sum[NUM_CORES];
volatile uint32_t done[NUM_CORES];

int main(void)
{
    uint32_t id = this_core_id();
    int first = id * SLICE;
    uint32_t sum = 0;
    ...
    for (i = first; i < first + SLICE; i++)
        data[i] = value_at(i);
    for (i = first; i < first + SLICE; i++)
        sum += data[i];

    partial_sum[id] = sum;
    done[id] = 1;

    if (id == 0)
    {
        uint32_t total = 0;
        for (k = 0; k < NUM_CORES; k++)
        {
            while (read_shared(&done[k]) == 0)
                ;
            total += read_shared(&partial_sum[k]);
        }
        *(volatile uint32_t*) TOTAL_ADDR = total;
        ...
    }
    report_and_halt(ok, 1);
}

The program shows three points.

  • Work divided by core ID. Every core runs the same code, and its ID alone picks its slice.
  • One writer for every shared word. partial_sum[k] and done[k] are written by core k only, so no lock is needed.
  • A join. Core 0 waits for each core's done flag before reading its partial sum. A core's stores reach memory in program order, so once done[k] reads 1, partial_sum[k] holds core k's sum. read_shared() reads both words with uncached loads, so core 0 never reads an old copy from its own cache.

The .vprj checks every core's result and the total that core 0 stores at 0x00100000.

RESULTS =
o0=0x00000001
o1=0x00000001
core1.o0=0x00000001
...
m[0x100000]=0x037ff800

docs.title: Parallel matrix multiply
docs.text:
parallel_matmul.c computes C = A x B for 16 x 16 integer matrices. Here the cores share real data. Core 0 produces both input matrices, every core reads them, and core 0 reads every core's part of the result.

int A[N][N], B[N][N], C[N][N];
volatile uint32_t inputs_ready;
volatile uint32_t done[NUM_CORES];

    //1. Core 0 produces the inputs, the others wait for them.
    if (id == 0)
    {
        ... fill A and B ...
        inputs_ready = 1;
    }
    else
    {
        wait_for(&inputs_ready);
        flush_caches();
    }

    //2. Every core computes its own block of rows.
    for (i = id * ROWS_PER_CORE; i < (id + 1) * ROWS_PER_CORE; i++)
        for (j = 0; j < N; j++)
        {
            int sum = 0;
            for (k = 0; k < N; k++)
                sum += A[i][k] * B[k][j];
            C[i][j] = sum;
        }
    done[id] = 1;

    //3. Core 0 gathers and checks the result.
    if (id == 0)
    {
        for (k = 0; k < NUM_CORES; k++)
            wait_for(&done[k]);
        flush_caches();
        ... check every element of C, store a checksum ...
    }

Two flags order the three steps. inputs_ready tells the other cores that A and B are complete, and done[k] tells core 0 that core k's rows of C are complete.

The flags alone are not enough when the caches are in use, because a core reads A, B and C with ordinary loads, which can hit its own cache. The program flushes its caches each time it starts to read data another core has produced.

  • Core 0's flush, before it reads C, is needed. Core 0 cleared .bss at startup, C included, so its cache can hold zeros for every row of C. Without the flush, core 0 reads those zeros instead of the other cores' rows. With caching on, the program then fails on both models.
  • The other cores' flush, before they read A and B, is a safeguard. Their caches have never held A or B in this program, so they cannot hold an old copy. A core that had read A before core 0 filled it in would need the flush.

With --coherent, the flushes are no longer needed, and the program is still correct as it stands.

docs.title: Building and running the examples
docs.text:
The examples build and run like any other test in the suite.

source compiler/toolchain_env.sh
validation/build_hex.py validation/multicore/examples
validation/run_tests.py validation/multicore/examples --config multicore
validation/run_tests.py validation/multicore/examples --config multicore --sitar

A single program can also be run directly, with its expected results.

cd model/system_models/multicore/sitar_model
SPARC_ALWAYS_CACHEABLE=1 ./executable/sparc_sim_sitar_multicore \
    ../../../../validation/multicore/examples/parallel_matmul/parallel_matmul.hex \
    ../../../../validation/multicore/examples/parallel_matmul/parallel_matmul.expected 5000000

On the sitar_model the caches make a large difference, because without them every instruction fetch of every core crosses the shared bus.

Program Cycles, nothing cached Cycles, SPARC_ALWAYS_CACHEABLE=1 parallel_sum about 3,086,000 about 467,000 parallel_matmul about 2,470,000 about 447,000

--stats prints, among the other counters, the number of bus transactions each core made. For parallel_matmul with caching on, cores 1 to 3 make about 8,400 each, and core 0, which also produces the inputs and checks the result, about 34,000.

docs.title: Execution Model
docs.text: Real cores run at the same time. A simulator has to decide how to run them, and the two models in this project decide differently. The difference matters when reading results. It decides what a "cycle" means in each model, how the peripheral devices keep time, and why a program can produce different results on the two models.

docs.title: The cpp_model: cores take turns
docs.text:
The cpp_model has no clock. It runs on one host thread, and executes one core's instruction at a time, to completion, before the next one starts. The cores therefore take turns, and a scheduler decides the order.

Execution proceeds in rounds. In each round, every running core gets one turn, in an order the scheduler picks, and executes some number of instructions in a row during it. The cores are thought of as running side by side during a round, so a round lasts as many model cycles as its longest turn. At the end of the round the peripheral devices tick once per model cycle of the round, and then every core's interrupt input takes the level the Interrupt Controller now presents for it.

Three scheduling strategies are available, chosen with --schedule (or the SPARC_SCHEDULE environment variable).

Strategy Order within a round Turn length rr:K (the default is rr:1) Round-robin. The core that goes first moves on by one every round, so no core is always first. K instructions rr-fixed:K Round-robin, with core 0 always first. K instructions random:S[:M] A random order of the running cores, each round. Random, 1 to M instructions (default M = 8)

The random strategy draws from a generator seeded with S, so the same seed always gives the same interleaving, on any host.

With one core and rr:1, a round is one instruction followed by one device tick, which is exactly how the single-core configurations run. The multicore cpp_model with one core running therefore reproduces core_l1cache_mmu_devices cycle for cycle.

Because each instruction runs to completion before any other starts, every instruction is atomic in the cpp_model. An LDSTUB or SWAP reads and writes memory with no other core able to come in between.

docs.title: The sitar_model: cores run side by side
docs.text:
In the sitar_model each core is its own Sitar module. All cores advance together, cycle by cycle, each executing at most one instruction per cycle. The cores meet only at the shared bus (see Model Structure and Assumptions), which serves one request at a time and grants the cores in round-robin order. A core whose request is waiting for the bus waits, while the others go on.

Every crossing of a net costs at least one cycle, so an access that leaves a core takes several cycles, and longer still when other cores are using the bus. A cache hit stays inside the core and costs no bus time at all. The peripheral devices tick once per cycle, and each core receives its interrupt level over its own net, one cycle after the Interrupt Controller changes it.

An LDSTUB or SWAP takes two bus transactions here, a read and then a write. The bridge keeps every other core off the bus between them, so the instruction is atomic in this model too (see The bus lock).

With --coherent, a write also sends an invalidate to every other core, which arrives in the cycle memory takes the write (see Coherence).

The effect of the shared bus can be seen directly. In the validation test multicore/boot/staggered_halt, core i counts to (i + 1) * 3000. With the MMU off nothing is cached, so every instruction fetch of every core goes through the bus.

Cores running Cycles until every core halts (no caching) 1 about 171,000 2 about 388,000 3 about 714,000 4 about 1,148,000

With caching turned on (SPARC_ALWAYS_CACHEABLE=1), four cores finish in about 147,000 cycles, because nearly every fetch then hits in each core's own cache.

docs.title: Why the two models can give different results
docs.text:
Each model interleaves the cores' memory accesses in its own way. In the cpp_model the scheduler alone decides the interleaving. In the sitar_model it follows from every instruction's latency and every wait at the bus. Even with every Sitar latency knob at 0, crossing a net still costs a cycle, so the two models never interleave the cores in exactly the same way.

  • A program whose result does not depend on the order in which the cores' accesses happen, such as one where each core works on its own data and the cores synchronize correctly, gives the same result on both models, and under every cpp scheduling strategy.
  • A program whose result does depend on that order, a program with a data race, can give different results on the two models, and on the cpp_model under different strategies or seeds. This is the behavior of real hardware too. The random strategy exists to expose such programs, by trying many interleavings.

A program's result can therefore be trusted only if it is the same under every interleaving. Running a test under several schedules is a quick way to check that.

docs.title: Devices and time in the cpp_model
docs.text: The single-core cpp_models have the same question to answer for the Timer, which counts time although the cpp_model has none. There, the devices tick once after every instruction, so one instruction is one model cycle and the timer counts instructions. The multicore cpp_model keeps that meaning for each core. A round lasts as long as its longest turn, so a timer set to fire after n cycles fires after each core has executed about n instructions, whatever the number of cores.

docs.title: OpenMP Programs
docs.text: A program for the multicore system can use real OpenMP pragmas. The cross compiler, sparc-elf-gcc 4.4, turns the pragmas into calls to a runtime library, and the toolchain has no such library for a bare-metal target. The header omp.h provides one, written for this project. It implements OpenMP 3.0, with the limits listed below.

docs.title: A first program
docs.text:
#include <omp.h>

int main(void)
{
    int i, sum = 0;

#pragma omp parallel for reduction(+:sum)
    for (i = 1; i <= 100; i++)
        sum += i;

    return sum;
}

The program needs two things from its build. The compiler option -fopenmp turns the pragmas on, and the startup file crt0_multicore.s brings up all the cores. In a test's .vprj these are two lines.

SOURCES = my_program.c
STARTUP = crt0_multicore.s
COMPILE_OPTIONS = -fopenmp
RUN_OPTIONS = --coherent

The same build by hand is as follows.

CRT0=crt0_multicore.s COMPILE_OPTIONS=-fopenmp $SPARC_HOME/compiler/compile_c.sh my_program.c
./executable/sparc_sim_cpp_multicore my_program.hex "" 5000000 --coherent

The compiler prints unrecognized option '-pthread', because -fopenmp asks for that option and this compiler has no threads library. The message is harmless.

The header holds the whole runtime, so the program includes it in its one source file, even if it calls no omp_ routine. Without it, the program does not link.

docs.title: How a program runs
docs.text:
The startup file calls main() on every core. The header defines main() itself and renames the program's own, so that only core 0 runs the program, as OpenMP expects. Cores 1 and up wait for work.

A parallel region's team of n threads is cores 0 to n-1, and a thread's number is its core's ID. Core 0 fills in a description of the team, and then wakes each worker through a word that only that worker waits on. At the end of the region, all the threads meet at a barrier, and the workers go back to waiting.

When the program's main() returns, the workers halt, and core 0 halts with the return value in %o0. The run then ends, since every core has halted. A program can also end with omp_end_program(o0, o1), which sets both registers, from outside any parallel region. A plain ta 0 is not enough, since it halts core 0 alone, and the run would go on until its cycle limit. Each worker halts with %o0 = 1, so a test can check that the workers stopped in an orderly way.

The header also turns the FPU on, on every core. The startup files leave it off, and a worker would have no chance to turn it on before running part of a region.

docs.title: How many threads
docs.text:
At startup, core 0 waits a bounded time for the other cores to report in. A core held back by --run-cores never does, so omp_get_num_procs() gives the number of cores really running, and a program run with --run-cores 1 still finishes, with every team having one thread. The wait comes only when a core is missing. The test on_one_core, which does little else, takes about 870 thousand cycles on the cpp_model.

A region gets as many threads as num_threads, omp_set_num_threads() or the default says, and never more than the number of cores. The default is one thread for each core.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
OpenMP's threads share memory, so a program's shared data must reach every core. There are two ways to run a program for which this holds.

Run Shared data Timing The default, MMU off and no options Nothing is cached, so every load sees main memory Every fetch and load goes over the bus, as in the other programs --always-cacheable --coherent Cached, and coherent The most realistic

With --always-cacheable alone a thread can read a stale copy of shared data, so a program gets wrong answers, and a loop waiting on a shared flag may never end. The tests all set RUN_OPTIONS = --coherent, so they are coherent whichever way they run.

#pragma omp flush compiles to STBAR, which orders stores in the model only as much as they are already ordered, since the model has no store buffer. It does not refresh a cached copy. Under --coherent it does not need to.

If a program turns the MMU on, its shared data must be identity-mapped, since the runtime's uncached reads take a physical address. This is the same limit as for the rest of the library.

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text: Feature Notes parallel, with if, num_threads, shared, private, firstprivate, reduction, copyin A nested region has a team of one. for, with schedule(static, dynamic, guided, runtime), ordered, lastprivate, nowait, collapse A plain schedule(static) is compiled inline, and its blocks are sized by the compiler. sections, single, copyprivate, master critical, named and unnamed, atomic, barrier, ordered, flush atomic takes one lock, since SPARC V8 has no compare-and-swap. task, taskwait Tasks run at once, on the thread that creates them. threadprivate Each core keeps its copies on its own stack, reached through %g7. omp_ routines for teams, levels, schedules and locks All of those in OpenMP 3.0, but for the clock routines.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Tasks give no speedup. A task runs when it is created, on the thread that creates it, which OpenMP allows. A program gets the right results, but all the tasks made by one single run on one core.
  • A nested region has a team of one, so omp_set_nested() has no effect. This is also what a host's OpenMP does by default. At most OMP_MAX_SERIAL_DEPTH (8) nested regions can be open at once. Going deeper ends the run with the code 0xBAD0E571 in %o0.
  • There is no omp_get_wtime(), since the system has no clock a program can read. The simulator reports cycles at the end of a run, so a program's timing is measured from outside.
  • omp_set_dynamic() has no effect. Teams always have the number of threads asked for, up to the number of cores.
  • Loops that need 64-bit iteration counts do not link, since GOMP_loop_ull_* is not provided.
  • OpenMP must not be used from an interrupt handler, like the rest of the library.
  • A program has one source file, as for every C program here, and the header goes in it.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
openmp_matmul.c multiplies two matrices with one pragma, where the same work done by hand needs flags and flushes.

#pragma omp parallel for private(j, k) schedule(static)
for (i = 0; i < N; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < N; j++)
    {
        int32_t sum = 0;
        for (k = 0; k < N; k++)
            sum += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
        c[i][j] = sum;
    }

The table gives the cycles for each team size, on the sitar_model with --always-cacheable --coherent. The program checks its answer by doing the same work again on core 0 alone. The last column is for a copy of the program with that check taken out.

Threads Whole program Without the check Speedup, without the check 1 3,338,310 1,848,091 1.00 2 2,489,576 1,060,430 1.74 3 2,210,160 760,176 2.43 4 2,098,131 666,029 2.77

The whole program gains far less, since about half of its single-thread run is the check, which no number of threads can shorten. Without the check, the speedup still falls short of the number of threads, since core 0 alone fills in the inputs, and all the cores share one bus.

To change the team's size, build with COMPILE_OPTIONS="-fopenmp -DTHREADS=2".

docs.title: How the runtime was checked
docs.text: The tests are in validation/multicore/openmp/ (see the validation suite). Each one is a self-checking program, and eleven of the fifteen also build with the host's gcc -fopenmp. The script check_on_host.py in that folder runs those eleven on the host with four threads and compares their results with what the .vprj files hold the simulators to. So those tests are checked against a real OpenMP implementation, and the runtime is checked against the tests.

docs.title: Parallel Simulation
docs.text: The sitar_model of the multicore configuration can run on several host threads at once, with each thread simulating some of the cores. The result of a parallel run is identical to the result of a serial run, cycle for cycle. The general page on Parallel Simulation explains why that holds, and when a parallel run is faster. This page covers how to build and run this configuration in parallel, and how its modules are divided among threads.

docs.title: Building and running
docs.text:
Parallel simulation needs an executable built with OpenMP.

cd model/system_models/multicore/sitar_model
./build.sh --openmp

This produces sparc_sim_sitar_multicore_openmp, alongside the serial executable. --openmp combines with --logging, which produces sparc_sim_sitar_multicore_logging_openmp.

The number of threads is set with --threads, or with OpenMP's own OMP_NUM_THREADS. Without either, the run uses one thread, since a small system runs slower in parallel (see Speed).

./executable/sparc_sim_sitar_multicore_openmp my_test.hex my_test.expected 5000000 --threads 2
OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 ./executable/sparc_sim_sitar_multicore_openmp my_test.hex

With one thread, the executable runs serially. The number of threads is limited to NUM_CORES, since a thread with no core of its own would only add work at every barrier. --stats prints which modules each thread ran.

=== threads ===
 2 thread(s):
     thread 0 = cores[0] cores[1]
     thread 1 = cores[2] cores[3] bridge mainMemory devices system

docs.title: Dividing the modules among threads
docs.text:
The units divided among threads are the modules directly under System. These are each cores[i], with its core, caches and MMU inside it, and the four modules that every core shares: bridge, mainMemory, devices, and system itself.

The division is static. A thread runs the same modules in every phase of the whole run (see Dividing the modules among threads).

docs.title: The default division
docs.text:
By default each thread takes a block of cores with consecutive numbers, as evenly as possible. When the cores do not divide evenly, the lower-numbered threads take one core more. The four shared modules do little work in a cycle, so they never get a thread of their own. They join the last of the threads with the fewest cores.

Cores Threads Default division 4 2 thread 0: cores 0 and 1. thread 1: cores 2 and 3, and the shared modules. 4 3 thread 0: cores 0 and 1. thread 1: core 2. thread 2: core 3, and the shared modules. 4 4 one core per thread, and the shared modules with core 3.

docs.title: Choosing the division
docs.text:
--thread-map gives the thread of every module, in the order --stats prints them: cores[0] to cores[NUM_CORES-1], then bridge, mainMemory, devices and system. The number of threads is then the largest thread number named, plus 1.

# cores 0 and 1 on thread 0, cores 2 and 3 on thread 1, shared modules on thread 0
./executable/sparc_sim_sitar_multicore_openmp my_test.hex --thread-map 0,0,1,1,0,0,0,0

A good division gives every thread about the same work per phase. The cores do most of the work. The shared modules are light, but the bridge and main memory serve every core's bus traffic, so with many bus transactions they add noticeably to their thread's load. A thread with the shared modules can then be given one core fewer than the others.

docs.title: Binding threads to host CPUs
docs.text:
OpenMP's own environment variables bind each thread to one host CPU for the whole run.

OMP_PROC_BIND=true OMP_PLACES=cores ./executable/sparc_sim_sitar_multicore_openmp ...

docs.title: When the run stops
docs.text: A run stops when System calls stop simulation, once every running core has halted (see The end of a run). Every thread leaves the parallel loop after the phase in which that call was made, so a parallel run ends on the same cycle as a serial run (see When the run stops).

docs.title: Logging in a parallel run
docs.text: A --logging build writes each core's instruction trace to its own file in a parallel run too, exactly as in a serial run (see Logging and Debugging). The Sitar module log is the one shared stream, and lines written to it from several threads would interleave. A parallel run therefore gives each thread its own module log, sitar.thread0.log, sitar.thread1.log, and so on, which hold the log lines of that thread's modules. sitar.log is then left empty.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: One SPARC core of this model does a fraction of a microsecond of work in a phase, about what a barrier costs. The multicore configuration, with 4 cores and the shared modules, has too little work per phase for 2 or more threads to gain. It runs a little slower in parallel than serially (see the measurements). Its parallel mode is therefore most useful as a check that a model keeps to Sitar's two-phase rule, and as a starting point for larger models, such as the 64-core speedup demonstration.

docs.title: Programming the Multicore System
docs.text: Every core starts at PC 0 and runs the same program. A multicore program is therefore one program that every core runs, which reads the core ID to decide what each core does. This page covers the startup file that prepares every core, how a program finds its core ID, how cores share data and wait for each other, with and without coherent caches, how each core takes its own interrupts, and the routines this project provides for all of this. Example Programs puts these pieces together in two complete programs.

docs.title: The startup file
docs.text:
C programs for the multicore configuration start from compiler/crt0_multicore.s, selected with a STARTUP line in the program's .vprj.

SOURCES = my_test.c
STARTUP = crt0_multicore.s

It is crt0_interrupts.s (see Writing and Running C Programs) with three additions.

  1. A stack for each core. Core i's stack starts at 0x0fffffa0 - i * 0x100000, so each core has 1 MB of stack of its own.
  2. One-time initialization by core 0. Core 0 clears .bss, the area of uninitialized global variables, before any core runs main().
  3. A release flag. When it has finished, core 0 writes 1 to word 0 of the Scratch-pad. The other cores wait for that value before calling main().

The scratch-pad holds the flag because it is a device, and devices are never cached. Every core therefore sees core 0's write at once, whatever the state of its own caches and MMU. Programs that use this startup file should leave scratch-pad word 0 alone.

Because crt0_multicore.s takes interrupts, a program using it must include ajit_mt_irc.h, which defines the interrupt dispatch function it calls.

docs.title: Finding the core ID
docs.text:
ajit_get_core_and_thread_id() (in compiler/include/ajit_access_routines.h) returns the core and thread ID from ASR29.

#include "ajit_access_routines.h"
#include "ajit_mt_irc.h"

int main(void)
{
    uint8_t core_id, thread_id;
    ajit_get_core_and_thread_id(&core_id, &thread_id);

    volatile uint32_t* results = (volatile uint32_t*) 0x00100000;
    results[core_id] = 0xA0 + core_id;   // each core writes its own word

    __asm__ __volatile__("ta 0");        // every core must halt
    return 0;
}

Each core then works on its own part of the data, chosen by its ID, and halts with ta 0 when it is done. The run ends once every core has halted.

docs.title: Sharing data between cores
docs.text:
Main memory is shared, so a value one core stores can be loaded by any other. Two properties of the caches decide how a program must go about it.

  • The caches are write-through. Every store goes to main memory at once, as well as to the core's own cache. A core's stores also reach memory in the order the program makes them, since a core has at most one access on the bus at a time.
  • By default, the caches are not coherent. A store by one core does not remove an old copy of that line from another core's cache. A core that has the line cached keeps reading its old copy. The --coherent option changes this (see Coherent caches), and this section describes a program written for the default.

Whether anything is cached at all is decided by the MMU. With the MMU off, as in the examples and tests here, nothing is cached unless the simulator's "always cacheable" option is set (SPARC_ALWAYS_CACHEABLE=1 or --always-cacheable). With the MMU on, the page tables decide. A program that works only with the caches out of the way is fragile, so the programs here are written to work either way, and the validation suite runs them both ways.

A core can make sure it reads what another core has written in three ways.

  1. An uncached load. A load with an MMU-bypass ASI never uses the cache. read_shared() (in multicore_core.h) reads a word this way. With the MMU off, a variable's address is its physical address, so read_shared(&flag) works on any global variable.
  2. A cache flush. flush_caches() (also in multicore_core.h) empties the core's own caches with a store to ASI 0x10. Every load after it comes from main memory, until the lines are cached again. This suits reading a large block of data that another core has produced.
  3. A device. Devices are never cached. The startup file's release flag lives in the scratch-pad for this reason.

Stores need no such care, because the caches are write-through.

docs.title: Waiting for another core
docs.text:
The simplest way for cores to coordinate is through flags, words that only one core ever writes. A core announces that something is ready by storing to its own flag, and another core waits by reading that flag until it changes.

// core k, after publishing its result:
partial_sum[k] = sum;
done[k] = 1;            // stores reach memory in order, so the sum is there first

// core 0:
while (read_shared(&done[k]) == 0)
    ;
total += read_shared(&partial_sum[k]);

The tests bound every wait with WAIT_LIMIT polls, so a program whose partner never answers fails its check instead of running until the cycle limit.

docs.title: Coherent caches
docs.text:
With the --coherent option, a store by one core removes that line from every other core's caches. A plain load then always returns the latest value, and none of the care above is needed. A program can be written as if the caches were not there. The test coherence/lock_and_counter_with_plain_loads does this, with a spinlock and a counter that use only plain loads.

./executable/sparc_sim_sitar_multicore my_test.hex --coherent

A program written for the default, with uncached loads or flushes, also runs correctly with --coherent. The reverse is not true. A program that relies on coherence fails without it, usually by waiting for ever on an old cached copy.

Coherence has a cost. A line that several cores write is removed from the others on each write, even when the cores use different words of it, which is called false sharing. Each core then misses more, though no value ever changes. The test coherence/false_sharing shows this. Data that different cores write often is better kept in separate lines, 64 bytes apart.

Two limits remain. A store does not update the writer's own instruction cache, so a core running code it has just changed must still execute FLUSH. Other cores need no flush for that code. A bypass store does not update the writer's own cached copy either, though it does remove other cores' copies.

Coherence works with the MMU on as well, whatever virtual addresses and contexts the cores use, because an invalidate goes by physical address. The tests in mmu_coherence/ cover the combinations.

docs.title: Locks and synchronization
docs.text:
A word written by more than one core needs a lock. Two cores incrementing the same counter can each read the old value and each write back one more, and one of the increments is lost. In the test atomics/counter_without_lock, four cores each add 1 to a counter 100 times. Running in step on the sitar_model, they end with a total of just 100, not 400. The cpp_model schedules that were tried give between 100 and 215, and none of them reaches 400.

A lock in turn needs an atomic instruction. SPARC V8 has two, and both are atomic across cores in both models (see The bus lock).

  • LDSTUB reads a byte and sets it to 0xFF. It returns 0 only if this core was the one that set it.
  • SWAP exchanges a word with a register.

The routines below are small inline functions in two headers in compiler/sparc_common_routines/, which compile_c.sh puts on the include path. multicore_core.h holds what the earlier sections use, and multicore_sync.h holds everything built on the atomic instructions.

docs.title: A mutex
docs.text:
A mutex is one byte or word in shared memory, and 0 means free. Global variables start at 0, so a mutex needs no setup.

#include "multicore_sync.h"

static volatile uint8_t  counter_lock;
static volatile uint32_t counter;

acquire_mutex_using_ldstub((int) &counter_lock);
counter = read_shared(&counter) + 1;
release_mutex_using_ldstub((int) &counter_lock);

The routines have the names and arguments of AJIT's own. While the lock is held, a waiting core spins on an uncached load, and tries the atomic instruction again only when the lock looks free. Spinning on the atomic instruction itself would lock the bus over and over and slow every other core.

Spinning on an uncached load is a deliberate difference from AJIT's routines, which spin with a plain load. Without coherent caches, a plain load could keep reading an old cached copy of the lock and never see it released. The routines work the same way with --coherent on or off.

docs.title: What a lock does not do
docs.text: This section applies when the caches are not coherent. A lock makes sure only one core is inside, but it does not refresh the cache. Inside the lock, a plain load can still return this core's old copy of the data. Data shared under a lock must be read with read_shared(), as above, or with a plain load after flush_caches() inside the lock, as the test sync_library/flush_inside_lock does.

docs.title: The other routines
docs.text:
Routine What it is for atomic_ldstub(), atomic_swap() The two instructions themselves. memory_fence() STBAR. It keeps earlier stores ahead of later ones. The model never reorders stores, so here it has no effect, but the architecture allows reordering, so a correct program uses it, as the release routines do. acquire_mutex_using_swap(), release_mutex_using_swap() A mutex in one word, using SWAP. try_acquire_mutex_using_ldstub() Takes the mutex only if it is free, and returns whether it did. atomic_fetch_and_add(), atomic_counter_read() An atomic_counter_t. SPARC V8 has no fetch-and-add instruction, so the counter has a lock byte of its own. ticket_lock_acquire(), ticket_lock_release() A ticket_lock_t. Unlike a mutex, it serves cores strictly in the order they arrived, so no core can be overtaken for ever. barrier_wait() A barrier_t. No core leaves until the given number of cores have arrived. It can be reused at once. semaphore_wait(), semaphore_try_wait(), semaphore_post() A semaphore_t, a count of free resources, initialized with SEMAPHORE_INITIALIZER(n).

Three limits apply to all of them.

  • They wait by spinning, without a limit, so a lock that is never released keeps a core spinning until the run's cycle limit.
  • Their uncached loads take a physical address. The MMU is off when a program starts, so this works as it is by default. A program that turns the MMU on must keep the locks and other shared structures at virtual addresses equal to their physical addresses, as the tests in mmu_coherence/ do.
  • They are not safe to use from an interrupt handler. A handler that waits for a lock its own core already holds waits for ever.

docs.title: Mixing LDSTUB and SWAP on one lock
docs.text: LDSTUB looks only at the byte it names, and the machine is big-endian, so byte 0 is the most significant byte of a word. A SWAP of the value 1 leaves that byte 0, and an LDSTUB on the same word would see the lock as free. A program that uses both on one lock must SWAP a value with the top byte set, as the test atomics/mixed_instructions does. The routines above use each lock with one instruction only, so they do not have this problem.

docs.title: Interrupts on several cores
docs.text:
The Interrupt Controller has a slot for each core, and core i takes its interrupts from slot 2i (see Interrupts). Each core enables its own slot, and the levels it wants, by writing its own slot's control register. Bit 0 enables the slot, and bit n lets level n through.

uint32_t id = this_core_id();
ajit_set_interrupt_handler(TIMER_IRL, timer_handler);
writeInterruptControlRegister(id, 0, (1u << TIMER_IRL) | 1u);

The table of handlers that ajit_set_interrupt_handler() fills in, ajit_global_interrupt_handlers, is one global array, shared by every core. Core 0 clears it with the rest of .bss. Every core can safely install the same handler for a level, since the writes agree. A handler that must act differently on each core reads the core ID itself.

  • Device interrupts. The Timer and the Serial device raise their level in every slot, and each slot's mask decides which cores take it. A core that leaves the timer's level out of its mask never sees the timer. The test interrupts/timer_to_selected_cores does this.
  • Inter-processor interrupts (IPIs). One core interrupts another through the controller's IPI block, using the routines in compiler/include/ajit_ipi.h. The sender enables the destination's IPI mask bit, then calls __ajit_set_ipi_interrupt__(), which writes an 8-byte message for the destination and sets its IPI value bit. The destination's handler reads the message and clears its value bit with __ajit_clear_ipi_interrupt__(). See Inter-processor interrupts for the registers.

The IPI routines change the shared mask and value words by read-modify-write. If two cores send IPIs at the same time, one core's change can be lost. The routines in the next section take care of this. A program that uses ajit_ipi.h directly should hold a mutex while sending an IPI, or send them from one core at a time, as the test interrupts/ipi_from_core0 does.

docs.title: Devices and the MMU across cores
docs.text: The header compiler/sparc_common_routines/multicore_platform.h holds what several cores need in order to share the devices and the page tables. A program includes it in place of ajit_mt_irc.h.

docs.title: A shared console
docs.text: One core calls console_start() once. After that, any core can call console_puts(), which prints a whole string under a lock, so that lines from different cores never mix. A run ends when every core has halted, so a program calls console_wait_until_sent() before halting, or its last character can be lost.

docs.title: Sending IPIs
docs.text:
Each core calls ipi_start_on_this_core() with its handler, before any core sends it an IPI. A core then sends with ipi_send(), and a handler reads the message and clears the IPI with ipi_receive().

static void handler(void)
{
    uint32_t source;
    void* pointer = ipi_receive(&source);
    // ...
}

int main(void)
{
    ipi_start_on_this_core(handler);
    // ...
    ipi_send(destination_core, some_pointer);

Both routines change the controller's registers under one lock. A handler needs that lock too, so a core holds it only with its interrupts off, using interrupts_off() and interrupts_restore(). Otherwise a handler could interrupt the core that holds the lock, and wait for it for ever. A sender whose destination has not yet taken its last IPI waits without the lock, since the destination's handler needs the lock in order to clear that IPI.

docs.title: TLB shootdown
docs.text:
Each core's TLB is its own, and a core goes on using its TLB's copy of a page table entry after another core has changed the entry in memory. Emptying the caches does not help. The test tlb_shootdown/stale_without_shootdown shows this. A core that changes an entry must therefore get every core to drop its copy.

tlb_shootdown_start_on_this_core();      // on each core, once
// ...
// On the core that changes the entry, after writing it to memory:
tlb_shootdown_page(va, context, NUM_CORES);

tlb_shootdown_page() drops this core's copy, sends an IPI to each of the others, and waits for each to answer. When it returns, no core can use the old translation. It returns the number of cores that did not answer, which is 0 unless a core has halted or has stopped taking interrupts. Only one shootdown runs at a time. A core waiting for its turn keeps its interrupts on, so it can take the one under way.

A handler drops a translation with a store using ASI 3, which also empties that core's L1 caches. A cached line of the old page therefore goes as well, even with coherence off.

docs.title: Limits of these routines
docs.text: The locks and the shootdown's shared words are reached at their physical addresses, so with the MMU on a program's data must be identity-mapped. The shootdown installs its own IPI handler, so a program cannot use it alongside IPIs of its own. A handler must not send IPIs or start a shootdown.

docs.title: Routines provided
docs.text:
Routine or name Where What it does ajit_get_core_and_thread_id() compiler/include/ajit_access_routines.h Reads the core and thread ID from ASR29. __ajit_load_word_mmu_bypass__(), __ajit_store_word_mmu_bypass__(), and byte versions compiler/include/ajit_access_routines.h Uncached loads and stores, by physical address. writeInterruptControlRegister(), enableInterrupt(), setInterruptMask(), and others compiler/include/ajit_mt_irc.h Set up a core's own Interrupt Controller slot. ajit_set_interrupt_handler() compiler/include/ajit_mt_irc.h Installs the handler for an interrupt level, in the table every core shares. __ajit_enable_ipi_interrupt__(), __ajit_set_ipi_interrupt__(), __ajit_clear_ipi_interrupt__(), ajitIpiMessageAddress() compiler/include/ajit_ipi.h Send, receive and clear inter-processor interrupts. this_core_id() compiler/sparc_common_routines/multicore_core.h This core's ID, as a number. read_shared(), read_shared_byte() compiler/sparc_common_routines/multicore_core.h Read a word or byte another core writes, with an uncached load. flush_caches() compiler/sparc_common_routines/multicore_core.h Empties this core's own L1 caches. Mutexes, atomic counter, ticket lock, barrier, semaphore compiler/sparc_common_routines/multicore_sync.h See Locks and synchronization. console_start(), console_puts(), console_wait_until_sent() compiler/sparc_common_routines/multicore_platform.h See A shared console. ipi_start_on_this_core(), ipi_send(), ipi_try_send(), ipi_pending(), ipi_receive() compiler/sparc_common_routines/multicore_platform.h See Sending IPIs. interrupts_off(), interrupts_restore() compiler/sparc_common_routines/multicore_platform.h Hold this core's maskable interrupts off, and let them back on. mmu_context(), mmu_set_context(), tlb_flush_page(), tlb_flush_entire() compiler/sparc_common_routines/multicore_platform.h Read or change this core's MMU context, and drop its own translations. tlb_shootdown_start_on_this_core(), tlb_shootdown_page() compiler/sparc_common_routines/multicore_platform.h See TLB shootdown. OpenMP's omp_ routines, and the runtime behind its pragmas compiler/sparc_common_routines/omp.h See OpenMP Programs. report_and_halt() validation/multicore/multicore_common.h Reports this core's checks in %o0 and %o1, and halts. finish_and_wait_for_all() validation/multicore/multicore_common.h Marks this core finished in a word of its own and waits for the others, so that every core can check a final result. NUM_CORES, SHARED_BASE, WAIT_LIMIT validation/multicore/multicore_common.h The number of cores the tests assume, a shared area for results at 0x00100000, and the bound on every wait loop.

The routines in compiler/include/ follow the names and signatures of AJIT's own access routines, so code written for AJIT compiles here unchanged. The interrupt levels' names, TIMER_IRL, IPI_IRL and SERIAL_IRL, are in compiler/include/device_addresses.h. multicore_common.h belongs to the validation suite. A program outside validation/multicore/ can include it by its path, or copy what it needs. The IPI routines of ajit_ipi.h write a message only once the destination is free, so an IPI not yet taken keeps its message.

A program can also leave the division of work to OpenMP's pragmas, which run on top of these routines. See OpenMP Programs.

docs.title: Model Structure and Assumptions
docs.text: This page describes how the multicore configuration is put together in each of its two models, and lists the assumptions the model makes where AJIT's own design was not followed or is not yet modeled. It builds on the single-core structure described in Model Configurations.

docs.title: The system
docs.text:
Every core of the multicore configuration is the core of core_l1cache_mmu_devices, with its own split L1 caches and its own MMU. Below the MMUs, one shared bus connects all the cores to one main memory and one set of peripheral devices.

  core 0          core 1          core 2          core 3
  L1 I/D caches   L1 I/D caches   L1 I/D caches   L1 I/D caches
  MMU             MMU             MMU             MMU
    |               |               |               |
  ==+===============+===============+===============+==  shared bus
                    |                       |
               main memory          peripheral devices
                (256 MB)      (Timer, Serial, Interrupt Controller,
                                         Scratch-pad)

A cache hit stays inside its core. A cache miss, every store (the caches are write-through), every uncached access, and every access to a device goes over the shared bus.

docs.title: The cpp_model
docs.text:
The cpp_model builds NUM_CORES copies of the single-core configuration's chain of C++ objects, one per core. Each copy holds a SparcCore, its SparcStateMachine, an L1CachesCore and an MmuCore. Every core's MmuCore is connected to the same SystemBus object, which sends each access to main memory or to the devices by its address, exactly as in the single-core configurations.

The cpp_model runs on one host thread. A Scheduler picks which core executes next and for how many instructions. Every access completes before the next one starts, so the bus never has two requests at once and needs no arbitration. The Execution Model page describes the scheduling strategies.

docs.title: Modules and nets
docs.text:
System holds NUM_CORES copies of the single-core configuration's Core module, as a Sitar submodule_array. Each Core contains the SPARC core, its L1 caches and its MMU as procedures, so a cache hit never leaves the core. Below the MMUs sits a CoherentBridge, the shared bus, and below it one main memory and one set of peripheral devices.

Top
 |
 +-- System (module)
      |
      +-- cores[NUM_CORES] : Core (module, one per core)
      |    |
      |    +-- sparcThread : SparcThread (procedure)
      |    |
      |    +-- caches : L1Caches (procedure)
      |    |
      |    +-- mmu : Mmu (procedure)
      |
      +-- bridge : CoherentBridge (module)
      |
      +-- mainMemory : PhysicalMainMemory (module)
      |
      +-- devices : PeripheralDevices (module)

Each core has three nets of its own, and the bus reaches memory and the devices over four more. Each net carries data from an output port to an input port.

Net From To coreRequestNet[i] cores[i].requestOut bridge.coreRequestIn[i] coreResponseNet[i] bridge.coreResponseOut[i] cores[i].responseIn interruptLevelNet[i] devices.interruptLevelOut[i] cores[i].interruptLevelIn memoryRequestNet bridge.memoryRequestOut mainMemory.requestIn memoryResponseNet mainMemory.responseOut bridge.memoryResponseIn devicesRequestNet bridge.devicesRequestOut devices.requestIn devicesResponseNet devices.responseOut bridge.devicesResponseIn

System sets each core's ID in its init block, so cores[i] is core i.

docs.title: The shared bus
docs.text:
CoherentBridge does the work of the single-core configuration's SystemBridge for several cores. It has one request port and one response port for each core. It takes one request at a time, reads its physical address, forwards it to main memory or to the devices, and returns the answer to the core that asked. Its timing is SystemBridge's, so with one core running, the multicore sitar_model reproduces core_l1cache_mmu_devices cycle for cycle.

When several cores have requests waiting, the bridge grants them in round-robin order. Starting from the port after the last one granted, it checks each port in turn, skips a port with no request waiting, and grants the first one that has a request.

The bridge is named after AJIT's coherent memory controller, which plays the same role.

docs.title: The bus lock
docs.text:
The bridge makes LDSTUB and SWAP atomic across cores. Each of these instructions reads a location and then writes it, and in the sitar_model those are two separate bus transactions, so another core could otherwise come in between them. The core's MMU marks the read with a lock bit, as AJIT's does.

A read with the lock bit set locks the bus to the core that made it, and that core's next request releases it. While the bus is locked, the bridge looks only at that core's port, so every other core's requests wait, whichever address they are for. As in AJIT's bridge, there is one lock for the whole bus, and it belongs to a core. This is coarser than atomicity strictly needs, since two atomic instructions on unrelated addresses need not exclude each other, but it is simple and it covers main memory and the devices alike.

The lock holds no extra time beyond the two transactions, so it changes no timing when only one core is using the bus. An access to an address that maps to nothing still takes and releases the lock, so it cannot leave the bus locked. --stats prints the number of locked read-write pairs the bridge has served.

docs.title: Coherence
docs.text:
With --coherent, a write to main memory removes that line from every other core's caches. Only the transport differs between the two models. The caches themselves are the same L1CachesCore class that every configuration uses, and in a single-core system nothing ever sends them an invalidate.

  • Finding a line. The caches are virtually indexed and tagged, but an invalidate carries a physical address. Each line therefore also keeps its physical address. A virtual and a physical address agree within a page, so only the sets the rest of the index could select need searching. In a 32 KB cache with 4 KB pages, that is 8 sets.
  • The sitar_model. When the bridge forwards a write to main memory, it pushes the line's address to every other core, on a net of its own, in that same phase. Each core polls this net every cycle, whatever it is doing, and again before every cache access, so a hit in that phase cannot see a line that has just been invalidated. The invalidate reaches the other cores in the same cycle that memory takes the write, before the writer gets its response.
  • The cpp_model. A small CoherentBus gives each core a port of its own onto the bus, and a write calls the other cores' caches directly. Nothing else is running at that moment, because the cores take turns.

A fill in progress. A line fill in the sitar_model is 8 separate bus reads, and another core can write the line between them. The invalidate then finds nothing to remove, since the line is not installed yet, and installing it would leave a stale line that nothing would ever remove. A cache therefore remembers the invalidates that arrive during a fill. If one of them is for this line, the fill still serves the read that started it, but the line is not installed. --stats counts these as fills abandoned.

The writer's own caches get no invalidate, as in AJIT. A store updates the writer's own data cache, but not its instruction cache, so code that modifies itself must still execute FLUSH.

Snoop filter. Every write sends an invalidate to every other core, since the bus cannot see which lines each cache holds. --snoop-filter leaves one out if that core's last invalidate was for the same line and it has read nothing from the bus since, because it cannot then hold the line. The results of a correct program do not change. Timing can change slightly, because the filter changes which fills in progress hear about a write, and so which of them are abandoned. --stats shows how many invalidates were left out. AJIT's bridge has a larger filter with the same purpose.

docs.title: Synonyms
docs.text: Two virtual addresses, or one address in two MMU contexts, can map to one physical line. A cache holds at most one copy of it, in every configuration. Installing a line first removes any older copy with the same physical address, so a store through one address is never missed by a load through the other. A store through an uncached alias and an atomic instruction never install a line, so they remove the other copy themselves. A store or atomic whose fault is suppressed by the MMU's NF bit reaches no memory and has no physical address, so it removes nothing. --stats counts these as synonyms removed. A bypass-ASI access goes around the cache on purpose, and leaves this core's own copy alone.

docs.title: Page table updates
docs.text: A successful translation sets the R bit of the page table entry, and a first write also sets its M bit. Both are written back to memory. With several cores, what the walk or the TLB holds may by then be out of date, and writing it back could undo a change another core has just made. So when more than one core runs, the MMU reads the entry again and sets the bits on what it finds, and an entry that is no longer a PTE is left alone. In the sitar_model the second read is locked, so the bus is held until the write. In the cpp_model each access runs to completion, so nothing can come between them. The second read costs a memory access, so it is left out with --run-cores 1, and in the single-core configurations, where nothing else writes the entry.

docs.title: The end of a run
docs.text:
In the single-core configurations, Core stops the simulation as soon as its core halts. Here a halted core only logs that it has halted, because the other cores may still be running. System watches every running core and stops the simulation once all of them have halted. It checks in the second phase of each cycle, after every core has finished its work for that cycle, so the cycle on which a run ends does not depend on the order in which the cores happen to run.

System's second parameter, STOP_WHEN_HALTED, is true by default. A model that holds several Systems sets it to false, since the first system to finish would otherwise end the run for all of them, and stops the run itself once every system has halted (see A larger model).

Cores beyond --run-cores are held in reset for the whole run, through SparcThread's reset pin, and the run does not wait for them.

docs.title: Latency knobs
docs.text: System.sitar's init block holds every latency knob. The per-core knobs (memory-interface delays, cache hit and fill delays, MMU delays) are set in a loop, the same for every core. The bus's bridge.delay, mainMemory.delay and the device knobs follow. All default to 0, as in the single-core configurations. See Model Configuration Settings for what each one does.

docs.title: Interrupts
docs.text:
The Interrupt Controller has 8 slots, one for each of 2 threads on each of 4 cores. Thread 0 of core i uses slot 2i. Every core here has one thread, so slots 0, 2, 4 and 6 are in use. Each core's interrupt input is driven from its own slot.

  • cpp_model. At the end of each scheduling round, every core's interrupt input takes the level its slot presents.
  • sitar_model. PeripheralDevices has one interrupt-level output for each of the 4 cores the controller supports, and System connects output i to core i. Each core polls its own net once per cycle. The single-core configurations connect output 0 only.

The controller's slot count is the reason NUM_CORES is at most 4.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
The model follows AJIT's multicore design wherever that design is known. The table lists where it makes its own assumptions, and what is not yet modeled.

Aspect In this model Notes Reset Every core starts at PC 0 and runs the same program. The reset PC is SparcCore's resetPC, which a model's main may change before the run. As in AJIT. Core ID ASR29 reads 0x50520000 \| (core << 8) \| thread. As in AJIT. One thread per core, so the thread field is 0. Threads per core 1 AJIT cores can have 2. Number of cores 1 to 4, set at compile time Limited by the Interrupt Controller's 8 slots. L1 caches Each core's own, VIVT, write-through, as in core_l1cache_mmu_devices Coherence Off by default, write-invalidate with --coherent See Coherence. Each line keeps its physical address, where AJIT keeps a separate reverse table (its RLUT). Data is the same either way, and only hit and miss counts differ. Synonyms At most one copy of a physical line per cache AJIT removes an older copy too, unless both have the same virtual address, in different contexts. Here that older copy is removed as well, since a store in one context would otherwise leave it stale. Memory ordering Sequentially consistent No store buffer. SPARC's TSO allows more than this, so correct programs still work. STBAR has no effect. Atomic LDSTUB and SWAP across cores Both models. The cpp_model runs each instruction to completion. In the sitar_model, the bridge locks the bus from the read to the write (see The bus lock), by core and for the whole bus, as in AJIT. Page table entry updates Atomic across cores, by a locked read and write in the sitar_model The R and M bits are set on the entry in memory, not on a copy. See Page table updates. Bus arbitration (sitar_model) Round-robin over the cores, one transaction at a time An assumption, not taken from AJIT. Bus timing (sitar_model) SystemBridge's, plus the bridge.delay knob Main memory and devices One of each, shared by every core As in AJIT. Interrupt routing Core i takes its interrupts from slot 2i As in AJIT, for thread 0. End of run When every running core has halted A modeling convenience. AJIT has no such notion.

docs.title: Validation Suite
docs.text: validation/multicore/ holds the programs that run on several cores at once. They assume the default build, with four cores. This page lists them, shows how each core's results are checked, and how to run the suite on both models. See Validation Suite for the test pipeline that every suite shares.

docs.title: Checking each core's results
docs.text:
Every core reports for itself, as the device tests do on one core. %o0 is 1 if every one of the core's checks passed, and %o1 has one bit per check. A test's .vprj names a core by prefixing a register with core<i>.. A register line without a prefix checks core 0, so every single-core test keeps working.

RESULTS =
o0=0x00000001
core1.o0=0x00000001
core2.o0=0x00000001
core3.o0=0x00000001
m[0x100000]=0x000000a0

Memory checks (m[...]) read main memory directly, which every core shares. The run ends once every core has halted, and a core that never halts makes the test fail when the cycle limit is reached.

The C tests start from crt0_multicore.s (their .vprj's STARTUP line) and include multicore_common.h (see Routines provided). The tests of the synchronization library also include multicore_sync.h.

docs.title: The tests
docs.text: Test Checks boot/release_flag_asm In assembly, without the startup file. Cores 1 to 3 wait on a release flag in the scratch-pad, set by core 0, then each core writes its own word of memory. Each core's ASR29 is checked too. boot/crt0_multicore What the startup file promises every core: its ASR29 value, its own stack region, .bss cleared, and the release flag set. Each core records its arrival in shared memory. boot/staggered_halt Core i counts to (i + 1) * 3000 before halting, so the cores halt far apart, and the run still waits for all of them. boot/deep_calls_mmu_on A call chain deeper than the register windows, with the MMU on. A window overflow writes above the stack pointer, so the startup file must leave room above its first one. interrupts/ipi_from_core0 Core 0 sends an inter-processor interrupt to each of cores 1 to 3 in turn. Each takes exactly one, with the right message, and core 0 takes none. interrupts/timer_to_selected_cores Cores 0 to 2 enable the timer's level and core 3 does not. Cores 0 to 2 each take exactly one timer interrupt, and core 3 takes none. interrupts/ipi_ping_pong Two pairs of cores pass an IPI back and forth at the same time. Every IPI arrives, from the right core, with the right pointer. interrupts/ipi_all_to_all Every core sends to every other core at once. All arrive, with message headers and pointers that agree, and each sender's in order. devices/console_under_lock Every core prints lines at once. They come out whole, in any order. devices/scratch_pad_across_cores A write by one core is seen by the others, also through the alias, and byte stores by different cores to one word all take effect. examples/parallel_sum The parallel array sum example. Checks each core's partial sum and the total. examples/parallel_matmul The parallel matrix multiply example. Checks every element of the product.

docs.title: Atomic instructions
docs.text:
The tests in atomics/ check LDSTUB and SWAP themselves across cores, with bare instruction loops rather than the library routines. Each is built so that a broken instruction shows up as a wrong final result, however the cores interleave.

Test Checks atomics/ldstub_counter Every core adds to one counter 100 times under a lock taken with LDSTUB. The total must be exact, or two cores were inside at once. atomics/ldstub_counter_asm The same test in assembly, without the startup file or the library. atomics/swap_counter The same with a lock taken with SWAP. atomics/ldstub_one_winner Every core does LDSTUB on each byte of a row. Exactly one core can read 0 from each byte, so the wins must add up to the number of bytes. atomics/swap_keeps_every_value Five different values are held by the cores and one shared word, and the cores keep swapping them. Each value must still exist exactly once at the end. atomics/ldstub_neighbour_bytes Each core uses LDSTUB on its own byte of one shared word, so a model that wrote back more than that byte would disturb a neighbour. atomics/mixed_instructions One lock, taken with LDSTUB, SWAP, LDSTUBA and SWAPA by different cores.
